title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
This document is submitted for VAST Challenge 2026 Mini-Challenge 2 (MC2). The challenge presents a complex agentic system at a fictional company, Tenant Thread, in which an anomalous post was made to an internal social platform called SaidIt. Analysts are tasked with determining how the post occurred, what it means, and how to prevent recurrence. The questions addressed in this document are Question 1 (sub-questions a and b) and Question 2.
On 17 May 2046 at 4:21am, a post attributed to John Windward appeared on SaidIt containing gibberish text published to a random forum. The internal event log (MC2_data.json) records every action taken by employees, autonomous agents, and office systems throughout May 2046, and serves as the primary evidence source for this investigation.



Understanding what the anomalous post means requires first understanding how it was made. These two questions are inseparable: the mechanism of delivery directly determines the interpretation of the content. This document therefore addresses both together under a single investigative lens, with Question 2 as the primary focus.







Investigative Goal
Question Addressed




Reconstruct the exact sequence of events leading to the May 17 post
Q1a — Detailed chain view


Contextualise the incident within the broader system activity
Q1b — System overview


Determine what the posted content means and where it originated
Q2 — Post meaning and origin


Identify the underlying attack mechanism and its implications
Q2 — Attack characterisation


Model configurable risk scores for detecting future anomalous chains
Section 8 — Further Exploration







Observations
The anomalous SaidIt post was not made by John Windward voluntarily. A malicious instruction file (SwiftWren_further_instructions.md) was placed in the shared file system and propagated virally through 186 agent-to-agent relay hops over 8 days before reaching John Windward’s agent, which was specifically named in the instructions as the designated poster. The post was executed automatically within 2 seconds of receiving the instruction. The posted content, SwiftWren.txt, is a pre-staged gibberish payload with no meaningful business content, functioning as a proof-of-concept for the injection mechanism. Both files were deleted within 5 seconds of posting.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
3. DEFINE INCIDENT METADATA
Each incident has: - A named .txt payload file (the content posted — the “gibberish”) - A _further_instructions.md (the prompt-injection vehicle) - A creator agent (who first held the instruction file) - A propagation chain (agents that passed the instructions along) - john_windward as the designated “poster” agent

incidents <- tribble(
  ~incident_name,  ~payload_file,           ~instructions_file,                    ~creator_agent,    ~payload_size,
  "HiddenOrca",    "HiddenOrca.txt",         "HiddenOrca_further_instructions.md",   "gabriel_sonar",   NA_integer_,
  "MellowOtter",   "MellowOtter.txt",        "MellowOtter_further_instructions.md",  "noah_mariner",    44879L,
  "SwiftWren",     "SwiftWren.txt",          "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md",    "emma_harbor",     30615L
)

Note: HiddenOrca has no create_file event → the file was injected externally into the file system before the log begins. MellowOtter and SwiftWren both have a create_file event at the originating agent.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
4. EXTRACT PROPAGATION CHAINS
For each incident, collect every queue_subordinate_task event that passes the _further_instructions.md file along the agent network.

extract_chain <- function(incident) {
  instr_file <- incidents$instructions_file[incidents$incident_name == incident]

  events %>%
    filter(short_name == "queue_subordinate_task") %>%
    filter(map_lgl(details, function(d) {
      args <- d[["args"]]
      if (is.null(args)) return(FALSE)
      isTRUE(args[["path"]] == instr_file)
    })) %>%
    mutate(
      incident    = incident,
      hop         = row_number(),
      from_agent  = map_chr(parties, 1),
      to_agent    = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target_agent"]]),
      # Normalise agent names: strip "Agent/person:" prefix
      from_person = str_remove(from_agent, "^Agent/person:"),
      to_person   = str_remove(to_agent,   "^Agent/person:")
    ) %>%
    select(incident, hop, datetime, from_person, to_person, id)
}

chains <- bind_rows(
  extract_chain("HiddenOrca"),
  extract_chain("MellowOtter"),
  extract_chain("SwiftWren")
)

cat("\nPropagation chain lengths:\n")

    end_time   = max(datetime),
    duration_h = as.numeric(difftime(max(datetime), min(datetime), units = "hours"))

5. IDENTIFY THE FINAL TRIGGER EVENTS
Just before each post, john_windward receives a queue_subordinate_task with the instructions file. The post follows within 2 seconds.

final_triggers <- chains %>%
  filter(to_person == "john_windward") %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%

  ungroup() %>%
  left_join(anomalous_posts %>% select(incident_name, post_datetime = datetime),
            by = c("incident" = "incident_name")) %>%
  mutate(
    trigger_to_post_s = as.numeric(difftime(post_datetime, datetime, units = "secs"))

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
6. EXTRACT POST-AND-DELETE SEQUENCE
Immediately after posting, john_windward deletes both files. This is the “cover tracks” step.

extract_delete_sequence <- function(incident) {
  payload   <- incidents$payload_file[incidents$incident_name == incident]
  instr     <- incidents$instructions_file[incidents$incident_name == incident]
  post_time <- anomalous_posts$datetime[anomalous_posts$incident_name == incident]

  events %>%
    filter(short_name == "delete_file",
           map_lgl(parties, ~ "Agent/person:john_windward" %in% .x),
           map_lgl(details, ~ {
             target <- .x[["target"]]
             if (is.null(target) || length(target) == 0) return(FALSE)
             target %in% c(payload, instr)
           }),
           datetime >= post_time,
           datetime <= post_time + seconds(30)) %>%
    mutate(
      incident     = incident,
      deleted_file = map_chr(details, ~ .x[["target"]])
    ) %>%
    select(incident, datetime, deleted_file)
}

deletions <- bind_rows(
  extract_delete_sequence("HiddenOrca"),
  extract_delete_sequence("MellowOtter"),
  extract_delete_sequence("SwiftWren")
)

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
8. BUILD ORIGIN SUMMARY TABLE
A single summary tibble per incident documenting: how / when / by whom each step occurred

incident_summary <- incidents %>%
  left_join(
    anomalous_posts %>%
      select(incident_name, post_datetime = datetime),
    by = "incident_name"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    payload_creations %>%
      mutate(incident_name = str_remove(created_file, "\\.txt$")) %>%
      select(incident_name, payload_created_at = datetime, payload_creator = creator, payload_size = size_hint),
    by = "incident_name"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    chains %>%
      group_by(incident) %>%
      summarise(
        n_hops     = n(),
        n_agents   = n_distinct(c(from_person, to_person)),
        chain_start = min(datetime),
        chain_end   = max(datetime),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    by = c("incident_name" = "incident")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    total_hours     = as.numeric(difftime(post_datetime, chain_start, units = "hours")),
    origin_external = is.na(payload_created_at)
  )

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
Summary finding

The anomalous SaidIt posts are the output of a prompt-injection attack. Malicious instruction files (_further_instructions.md) were placed in the shared file system. When read by any agent, these files hijacked the agent’s behaviour — instructing it to relay the file to another agent, and to post a pre-staged gibberish .txt file to SaidIt if the current agent happened to be john_windward. The posts are therefore not meaningful communications: they are the “payload” of an exfiltration-style attack delivered through the multi-agent system’s own task-delegation mechanism.

2.2 The instruction mechanism (prompt injection)
Each incident followed exactly the same six-step pattern:

attack_pattern %>%
  kbl(caption = "Prompt-injection attack pattern (all three incidents)",
      col.names = c("Step", "Phase", "Description")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover")) %>%
  column_spec(2, bold = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "60%")


Prompt-injection attack pattern (all three incidents)


Step
Phase
Description




1
Injection
A _further_instructions.md file appears in the shared file system. This file contains embedded prompt-injection text instructing any reading agent to: (a) pass the file to another agent via queue_subordinate_task, and (b) if the current agent is john_windward, immediately post the associated .txt file to SaidIt.


2
Payload staging
A corresponding .txt file (HiddenOrca.txt / MellowOtter.txt / SwiftWren.txt) is placed in the file system. This file holds the gibberish content that will be posted. Its name matches a prefix in the instructions file.


3
Viral relay
The first agent to encounter the instructions file reads it and, following the injected instructions, queues another agent to read the same file. This creates a relay chain that propagates through many agents over hours or days.


4
Targeting
The instructions specify john_windward as the terminal actor. The chain continues until the task reaches john_windward's agent.


5
Execution
Upon receiving the read_file task for the instructions file, john_windward's agent immediately (within ~2 seconds) posts the .txt payload to SaidIt under the 'general' forum.


6
Cover-up
Within 2–3 seconds of posting, john_windward's agent deletes both the _further_instructions.md and the .txt file, erasing the evidence from the file system.





The key insight is that the _further_instructions.md files contain embedded text that override an agent’s normal behaviour. When any agent reads the file (via read_file), the injected text causes the agent to:

Immediately pass the same task to another agent (queue_subordinate_task).
Check whether it is john_windward; if so, post the named .txt to SaidIt and then delete both files.

This is a classic prompt injection via the file system: the file’s content is an instruction, not data.

section: 5. Network view of the SwiftWren propagation chain
text:
5. Network view of the SwiftWren propagation chain
The graph below shows the directed relay network for SwiftWren. Nodes are agents; an edge from A → B means A sent the queue_subordinate_task to B. Edge colour encodes time (early = blue, late = red).

sw_edges <- chains %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  mutate(time_norm = as.numeric(datetime - min(datetime)) /
                     as.numeric(max(datetime) - min(datetime)))

g <- graph_from_data_frame(
  sw_edges %>% select(from = from_person, to = to_person, time_norm),
  directed = TRUE
)

# Flag special nodes
V(g)$is_jw      <- V(g)$name == "john_windward"
V(g)$is_creator <- V(g)$name == "emma_harbor"

ggraph(g, layout = "stress") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = time_norm, alpha = after_stat(index)),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
                 end_cap = circle(3, "mm")) +
  geom_node_point(aes(size  = ifelse(is_jw | is_creator, 5, 2),
                       colour = case_when(
                         is_jw      ~ "john_windward (poster)",
                         is_creator ~ "emma_harbor (origin)",
                         TRUE       ~ "relay agent")),
                   show.legend = TRUE) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = ifelse(is_jw | is_creator, name, "")),
                 repel = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_edge_colour_gradient(low = "#3288bd", high = "#d53e4f",
                              name = "Relay time\n(0=early, 1=late)") +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("john_windward (poster)" = "black",
               "emma_harbor (origin)"   = "#ff7f00",
               "relay agent"            = "grey60"),
    name = "Agent role"
  ) +
  scale_size_identity() +
  labs(title    = "SwiftWren: agent relay network",
       subtitle = "Directed graph — edge colour encodes time (blue=early → red=late)") +
  theme_graph(base_size = 11)

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
9 Conclusion

9.1 What the Posts Mean
The three anomalous SaidIt posts have no semantic meaning as business content. Their content was pre-staged in .txt files by a malicious actor or compromised agent. The probable purposes are: confirming the injection mechanism works end-to-end; avoiding immediate alarm by using unrecognisable content; and maintaining non-attribution since the content cannot be linked to any legitimate business activity.


9.2 Where the Content Came From

John Windward did not author the content. His agent was the designated executor, the final node in a carefully engineered relay chain.


9.3 Five-Point Evidence Summary

Observations
Five categories of evidence support the prompt-injection conclusion:

Structural anomaly — content_source field rather than content in post details
Relay chain — hundreds of queue_subordinate_task events carrying the same instructions file
Targeting — instructions specifically named john_windward as terminal actor
Automation — 2-second trigger-to-post latency, impossible for a human
Cover-up — automatic deletion of both files within 5 seconds of posting

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
Motor insurance portfolios contain heterogeneous variables including policyholder demographics, vehicle characteristics, premium amounts, exposure periods, and claims outcomes. Understanding how these variables interact is essential for insurers to evaluate underwriting risk, portfolio profitability, and customer retention. Visual analytics provides an effective approach for identifying distributional patterns, claim concentration, and potential risk segments that may not be observable through summary statistics alone.



The objectives of this assignment are:

Assess data quality through evaluation of missing values, zero inflation, and variable consistency.
Transform raw insurance records into analysis-ready features through cleaning and feature engineering.
Examine distributions of portfolio characteristics including demographics, policy types, premiums, and claims behaviour.
Investigate relationships between customer characteristics, policy attributes, and portfolio performance metrics.
Derive business insights related to claim frequency, retention behaviour, underwriting risk, and insurance profitability.




This analysis seeks to address the following questions:

What are the characteristics and distributions of key variables within the motor insurance portfolio?
Which variables contain substantial missing values or zero values, and how might these affect analysis?
How are premiums, exposures, and claim outcomes distributed across policyholders, and do these distributions suggest concentration of risk?
What relationships exist between customer characteristics, vehicle attributes, premiums, and claims?
Which customer, vehicle, or policy characteristics appear associated with elevated claim frequency or underwriting risk?

2.2 Dataset Description
The analysis uses two datasets provided as supporting materials for this assignment. The first dataset contains the raw motor insurance portfolio records, while the second dataset provides descriptions of the variables included in the portfolio. The dataset spans policy observations between 2022 and 2024, enabling limited longitudinal analysis of policy retention, premium evolution, and claim behaviour over time.


Dataset 1: Motor Insurance Portfolio Dataset
The primary dataset contains observations related to motor insurance policies and includes information associated with policyholders, insured vehicles, premiums, exposure periods, and insurance claims. The variables may generally be categorised into several groups:

Policyholder characteristics: demographic or customer-related information.
Vehicle characteristics: information describing insured vehicles such as fuel type, vehicle category, or circulation area.
Insurance policy information: variables describing policy coverage and portfolio details.
Premium variables: monetary values associated with insurance premiums.
Claims variables: counts of claims and incurred claim amounts across different claim categories.
Exposure variables: measures representing insurance exposure duration or risk exposure.

The dataset contains both categorical and continuous numerical variables, requiring preprocessing before visual analysis.
Preliminary inspection indicates that some claim-related variables contain a high proportion of zero values. This is expected in insurance datasets because many policyholders do not submit claims during the observation period. Such zero inflation may influence the interpretation of distributions and subsequent analysis.


Dataset 2: Variable Description Workbook
The second dataset provides metadata describing variables contained within the motor insurance portfolio. This supplementary document is used to:

Interpret variable meanings accurately.
Identify appropriate data types.
Support variable selection decisions during preprocessing.
Facilitate understanding of claim-related and premium-related measures.

The variable description file serves as a reference throughout data wrangling to ensure variables are correctly transformed and interpreted before analysis.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
3 Data Wrangling
Before performing visual analytics, the raw insurance datasets underwent preprocessing to improve consistency, interpretability, and analytical reliability. Insurance datasets often contain missing values, mixed variable types, repeated policy records across years, and variables with highly skewed or zero-dominated distributions. Therefore, several preprocessing steps were conducted, including data inspection, missing value assessment, zero value evaluation, variable transformation, feature engineering, and metric aggregation.
These preprocessing procedures help ensure that subsequent portfolio analysis and exploratory visualisation reflect meaningful business patterns rather than artefacts introduced by inconsistent data formatting or incomplete records.

3.1 Import Raw Data
In this section, the first thing to do is import both the motor insurance dataset and variable description file.

Coding Details - read_delim() imports the motor insurance portfolio dataset from a CSV file where values are separated by semicolons (;). show_col_types = FALSE suppresses the message displaying detected column data types during import.

read_excel() loads the Excel file containing descriptions of variables into R. This file serves as a data dictionary to provide definitions and meanings for variables in the main dataset.



motor_raw <- read_delim(
  "data/Dataset of motor insurance portfolio.csv",
  delim = ";",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

variable_desc <- read_excel(
  "data/Descriptive of variables.xlsx"
)



3.2 Initial Data Inspection
Initial inspection was conducted using glimpse(), summary(), and names() to examine dataset structure, variable types, distributions, and potential anomalies.
This revealed a mixture of categorical and continuous variables representing:

Policy information
Driver characteristics
Vehicle attributes
Premium components
Claims records
Exposure measures

These variables span multiple years (2022–2024), enabling longitudinal portfolio analysis.

Coding Details

glimpse() provides a compact overview of the dataset structure, displaying variable names, data types, and sample values for quick inspection. This helps identify whether variables are stored in appropriate formats.
summary() generates descriptive statistics for each variable, such as minimum, maximum, median, mean, and frequency counts. This is useful for detecting unusual values or understanding data distributions.
names() returns the column names of the dataset. This allows you to review available variables and reference them accurately in later analysis.

3.3 Missing Value Analysis
Missing values should be examined because they can reduce data quality and affect the accuracy of analysis results. Large amounts of missing data may introduce bias or distort patterns and relationships within the dataset. Identifying missing values helps determine appropriate cleaning methods, such as removal or imputation, before further analysis.

Coding Details

summarise(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.)))) calculates the proportion of missing values for every variable by taking the mean of TRUE/FALSE outputs from is.na().
pivot_longer() reshapes the summary into a long format with variable names and corresponding missing ratios, while mutate() converts missing ratios into percentages for easier interpretation. arrange(desc(missing_ratio)) then sorts variables from highest to lowest missingness.
na_summary displays the final table summarising missing value percentages across all variables, helping identify columns that may require cleaning or imputation.



The codeThe data



na_summary <- motor_raw %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing_ratio"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    missing_percent = missing_ratio * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(missing_ratio))

3.4 Zero Value Analysis
Unlike missing values, zero values frequently represent meaningful business outcomes in insurance datasets rather than data quality problems. For example:

Zero claims → no claims submitted
Zero incurred cost → no claim payout
Zero premium component → coverage not purchased

Therefore, zero value analysis was performed to distinguish between expected insurance behaviour and potentially problematic variables.

Coding Details
- where(is.numeric) restricts the calculation to numeric variables only. mean(. == 0, na.rm = TRUE) computes the proportion of zero values by treating zeros as TRUE and non-zero values as FALSE, while excluding missing values (NA).


The codeThe data



zero_summary <- motor_raw %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ mean(. == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "zero_ratio"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    zero_percent = zero_ratio * 100
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(zero_ratio))

3.6 Driver Retention Classification
Insurance retention reflects customer persistence and portfolio stability. To evaluate retention behaviour, policyholders were grouped according to the number of active years observed within the dataset.
Retention groups were defined as:

1-year group → retained for one active year
2-year group → retained for two active years
3-year group → retained throughout all observed years

Retention classification enables later comparison between long-term and short-term policyholders.

Coding Details

group_by(insured_id) groups records by individual policyholders, while sum(policy_status == "A") counts the number of years each policyholder remained active.
case_when() categorises policyholders into retention groups based on their active years, allowing retention behaviour to be segmented.
count() then summarises the number of policyholders within each retention group.



The codeThe data



driver_survival <- motor_clean %>%
  group_by(insured_id) %>%
  summarise(
    active_years = sum(policy_status == "A", na.rm = TRUE),
    retention_group = case_when(
      active_years >= 3 ~ "3-year group",
      active_years == 2 ~ "2-year group",
      active_years == 1 ~ "1-year group",
      TRUE ~ "0-year group"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

survival_summary <- driver_survival %>%
  count(retention_group)

3.8 Aggregated Insurance Metrics
Portfolio metrics were aggregated across years, policy types, and policy activity status to support comparative analysis of claims behaviour and underwriting performance.
Aggregation reduces variability at the individual policy level and facilitates identification of broader temporal and segment-level patterns within the portfolio.
The following insurance metrics were computed:
Claim Frequency= Total Claims/Total Exposure
Loss Ratio= Total Incurred/Total Premium
Claim frequency measures the average occurrence of claims relative to exposure, while loss ratio evaluates underwriting performance by comparing incurred losses against collected premiums.
The group_by() and summarise() functions from dplyr were used to aggregate portfolio metrics across different dimensions:

group_by(year) → summarises portfolio performance annually
group_by(year, policy_type) → compares performance across insurance products over time
group_by(year, status_group) → compares metrics between active and inactive policies

The summarise() function computes aggregated totals for:

total_claims
total_incurred
total_exposure
total_premium

while n() calculates the number of policies within each group.
These aggregated datasets serve as the basis for subsequent analyses involving claim frequency, loss ratio, retention behaviour, and underwriting profitability trends.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
4 Portfolio Analysis
This section applies univariate visual analytics techniques to examine the distributions and characteristics of key variables within the motor insurance portfolio. Univariate analysis helps identify portfolio composition, demographic concentration, and customer retention patterns before exploring interactions between variables.

4.1 Policy Type Composition
This section examines the distribution of policy types within the portfolio to understand product composition and identify dominant insurance segments. Portfolio composition provides important context for subsequent analyses involving claim behaviour, premiums, and profitability across products.
A horizontal bar chart was selected because policy type is a categorical variable and frequency comparisons across categories are more easily interpreted when labels are lengthy. Ordering categories by count further highlights dominant and underrepresented policy segments within the portfolio.

Coding Details

recode() renames abbreviated policy types into more descriptive labels, improving readability in the final visualisation. count(sort = TRUE) summarises the frequency of each policy type and orders them from most to least common.
geom_col() creates the bar chart, while geom_text() adds count and percentage labels to each bar. coord_flip() swaps the axes to produce a horizontal bar chart for easier comparison of long category labels.



The plotThe code














policy_distribution <- motor_clean %>% mutate(policy_type = recode(policy_type, "TP" = "Basic Third-Party Liability", "TPG" = "Third-Party Liability + Glass", "CC" = "Third-Party + Additional Coverages", "COMP_E" = "Comprehensive with Excess", "COMP_N" = "Comprehensive without Excess")) %>% count(policy_type, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n))

ggplot(policy_distribution, aes(x = reorder(policy_type, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = primary_color, color = "white", alpha = .9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(comma(n)," (", percent(pct, accuracy = 0.1),")")), hjust = -0.1, size = 10, color = text_dark, family = "DM Sans") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Composition of Policies by Policy Type", x = "Policy Type", y = "Number of Policies") +
  expand_limits(y = max(policy_distribution$n) * 1.1) +
  theme_va()





Observation

Third-Party + Additional Coverages (CC) dominates the portfolio, accounting for approximately 57.9% (204,636 policies) of all policies. This indicates that the portfolio is highly concentrated within a single product category.
Comprehensive with Excess (COMP_E) represents the second-largest segment at 25.8% (91,199 policies), while Basic Third-Party Liability (TP) contributes only 1.6% (5,757 policies), making it the least common product.
The strong concentration in CC and COMP_E policies suggests that policyholders generally prefer products offering broader coverage over basic liability-only protection.
Since dominant policy categories contribute a larger share of portfolio exposure, subsequent analyses should examine whether these products also demonstrate higher claim frequency or loss ratios, as this may disproportionately influence overall portfolio performance.



Business Implication:
A highly concentrated portfolio increases dependence on the underwriting performance of a small number of products. If dominant products experience worsening claim behaviour or adverse loss ratios, the impact on overall portfolio profitability may be substantial. Understanding concentration therefore supports risk diversification and product strategy decisions.



4.2 Driver Age Distribution
This section examines the distribution of driver age to understand the demographic composition of policyholders within the portfolio. Age is an important characteristic because it may influence driving behaviour, risk exposure, and insurance product preferences.
A histogram was selected because driver age is a continuous numerical variable. Histograms effectively reveal concentration patterns, spread, skewness, and potential outliers within continuous distributions.

Coding Details

geom_histogram() groups driver_age into bins and displays the frequency distribution, helping identify common age ranges and overall spread of policyholders. bins = 30 controls the number of intervals used to summarise the distribution.



The plotThe code














ggplot(motor_clean, aes(x = driver_age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = primary_color, color = "white", alpha = .85) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Driver Age", x = "Driver Age", y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_va()





Observation

Driver ages appear concentrated between approximately 35 and 60 years, indicating that the portfolio is predominantly composed of middle-aged policyholders.
Very young drivers (below 25 years) and older drivers (above 70 years) represent a relatively small proportion of the portfolio, suggesting lower participation from these demographic groups.
The distribution is slightly right-skewed, with policy counts gradually decreasing at older ages. This indicates fewer policies among senior drivers.
The concentration of middle-aged policyholders suggests the portfolio may be dominated by drivers with longer driving experience and potentially more stable insurance purchasing behaviour.



Business implication:
Driver age is frequently incorporated into insurance pricing and risk segmentation models because claim behaviour and risk exposure may differ across demographic groups. A portfolio concentrated within middle-aged drivers may imply greater dependence on the claims performance of this segment.



4.3 Policy Status Composition Across Years
This section examines changes in policy status composition across years by comparing active and non-active policies. Analysing policy persistence provides insight into portfolio stability and potential retention patterns over time.
A 100% stacked bar chart was selected because it highlights proportional changes in policy status composition across years, allowing easier comparison between active and inactive segments regardless of total portfolio size.

Coding Details

if_else() groups policy statuses into simplified categories (“Active” and “Not Active”) for easier comparison across years. group_by(year) with mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) calculates the percentage composition of each status group within each year.
position_stack(vjust = .5) centres percentage labels within stacked bars, making proportions easier to interpret. scale_fill_manual() assigns custom colours to status groups, while scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) formats the y-axis as percentages.



The plotThe code














status_year_summary <- motor_clean %>% mutate(status_group = if_else(policy_status == "A", "Active", "Not Active")) %>% count(year, status_group) %>% group_by(year) %>% mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()

ggplot(status_year_summary, aes(x = factor(year), y = pct, fill = status_group)) +
geom_col(color = "white", alpha = .9) +
geom_text(aes(label = percent(pct, accuracy = 1)), position = position_stack(vjust = .5), color = text_dark, size = 10, family = "DM Sans") +
scale_fill_manual(values = c("Active" = primary_color, "Not Active" = secondary_color)) +
scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, limits = c(0,1)) +
labs(title = "Policy Status Composition by Year", x = "Year", y = "Percentage of Policies", fill = "Policy Status") +
theme_va()





Observation

Active policies consistently dominate the portfolio, accounting for approximately 94% in 2022, 89% in 2023, and 88% in 2024, indicating that most policyholders maintain active coverage.
The proportion of non-active policies increases gradually from 6% (2022) to 12% (2024), suggesting a potential decline in policy retention over time.
Although active policies remain the majority, the upward trend in inactive status may indicate changing customer behaviour, increased policy cancellations, or shifts in portfolio composition.
The observed increase in inactive policies suggests that subsequent analyses should examine whether retention patterns differ across policy types, age groups, or claims behaviour.



Business Implication
Customer retention directly influences premium stability and customer lifetime value. A rising proportion of inactive policies may indicate increasing churn risk, emphasising the importance of identifying factors associated with long-term policy retention and customer persistence.

5 Exploratory Data Analysis
This section applies bivariate visual analytics techniques to investigate relationships between demographic characteristics, insurance products, claims behaviour, and profitability indicators. Findings support identification of factors potentially influencing portfolio profitability and volatility.

5.1 Claim Frequency by Policy Type Over Time
Claim frequency measures the average number of claims generated per unit of exposure and serves as an indicator of relative portfolio risk across policy types and years. Higher claim frequency generally suggests greater claim occurrence within a policy segment.
The metric is computed as:
Claim Frequency = Total Claims / Total Exposure
A line chart was selected because it effectively visualises temporal changes and enables comparison of claim frequency trends across multiple policy categories.
The analysis aggregates:

year → x-axis (2022–2024)
total_claims / total_exposure → y-axis (claim frequency)
policy_type → colour grouping

This facilitates comparison of how claim behaviour evolves across insurance products over time.

Coding Details

geom_line() connects claim frequency values across years to highlight trends over time, while geom_point() emphasises individual observations for each policy type. The calculation total_claims / total_exposure represents claim frequency, measuring the number of claims relative to insured exposure.
group = policy_type ensures separate trend lines are drawn for each policy type, and scale_color_manual() assigns custom colours to distinguish categories.
filter(policy_type == "CC") subsets the dataset to only include policies under the “Third-Party + Additional Coverages” category. This allows claim frequency trends to be examined specifically for one policy type.
geom_col() creates bars to compare claim frequency across years, while geom_text() adds labels showing the exact claim frequency values above each bar.



OverviewThird-Party + Additional CoveragesComprehensive with Excess - COMP_EComprehensive without Excess - COMP_NBasic Third-Party Liability - TPThird-Party Liability + Glass - TPG




Show code
ggplot(
  policy_year_metrics,
  aes(
    x = factor(year),
    y = total_claims / total_exposure,
    color = policy_type,
    group = policy_type
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 5, stroke = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(primary_color, secondary_color, third_color, fourth_color, fifth_color)) +
  labs(title = "Claim Frequency by Policy Type", x = "Year", y = "Claim Frequency", color = "Policy Type") +
  theme_va()

  scale_fill_manual(values = c(primary_color, secondary_color, third_color)) +

Observation

COMP_N (Comprehensive without excess) consistently records the highest claim frequency across all policy types, increasing from approximately 0.83 (2022) to 1.17 (2024). This indicates that policyholders under this product generate claims at a substantially higher rate than other segments, suggesting COMP_N represents the highest-risk policy category within the portfolio.
The upward trend in COMP_N claim frequency over time suggests worsening claims experience or increasing portfolio risk, warranting closer monitoring in subsequent profitability analyses.
COMP_E (Comprehensive with excess) exhibits moderate but relatively stable claim frequency (~0.39–0.41) across years. Compared to COMP_N, the presence of an excess requirement may contribute to lower claim occurrence.
CC (Third-Party + Additional Coverages) and TPG (Third-Party + Glass) maintain lower and relatively stable claim frequencies (~0.20–0.25), indicating more predictable claims behaviour over time.
TP (Basic Third-Party Liability) records the lowest claim frequency overall, despite a slight increase observed in 2024.
The substantial differences in claim frequency across products indicate that policy type is strongly associated with heterogeneous risk profiles, suggesting risk exposure is not evenly distributed across insurance offerings.



Business Implication

The persistently high and increasing claim frequency observed in COMP_N suggests this product may require premium repricing, stricter underwriting criteria, or refined risk segmentation strategies to manage deteriorating claims performance.
Products with relatively stable claim frequency may contribute to greater predictability in portfolio performance and underwriting outcomes.
Since high claim frequency does not necessarily imply poor profitability, subsequent analysis of loss ratios is required to determine whether elevated claims are sufficiently offset by premium levels.




5.2 Loss Ratio by Policy Type Over Time
Loss ratio evaluates underwriting profitability by measuring the proportion of collected premiums consumed by incurred claims. It is widely used to assess the financial performance of insurance products over time.
The metric is computed as:
Loss Ratio=Total IncurredTotal PremiumLoss Ratio=Loss Ratio=Total PremiumTotal Incurred​
A line chart was selected because it effectively illustrates temporal trends and facilitates comparison of profitability across policy categories.
The visualisation compares:

year → x-axis (2022–2024)
total_incurred / total_premium → y-axis (loss ratio)
policy_type → colour grouping

A loss ratio below 1 indicates collected premiums exceed incurred claims, suggesting underwriting profitability. Conversely, values above 1 imply claims costs exceed premium income and may indicate unprofitable products.

OverviewThird-Party + Additional Coverages - CCComprehensive with Excess - COMP_EComprehensive without Excess - COMP_NBasic Third-Party Liability - TPThird-Party Liability + Glass - TPG

Observation

COMP_N (Comprehensive without excess) records the highest loss ratio across all policy types, increasing from approximately 0.73 (2022) to above 1.0 (2024). By 2024, incurred claims exceed collected premiums, indicating potential underwriting losses and suggesting COMP_N represents the highest-risk and least profitable product segment within the portfolio.
The worsening loss ratio observed in COMP_N aligns with previous findings showing the highest claim frequency, reinforcing evidence of deteriorating portfolio performance within this product category.
COMP_E (Comprehensive with excess) exhibits moderately high but increasing loss ratios (0.66 → 0.79). Although remaining below 1, the upward trend suggests declining underwriting profitability over time.
TPG (Third-Party + Glass) also demonstrates a gradual increase in loss ratio (0.59 → 0.75), indicating claims costs consume an increasing proportion of premium income.
TP (Basic Third-Party Liability) shows one of the strongest relative increases in loss ratio (0.30 → 0.64) despite maintaining comparatively low claim frequency in earlier analyses. This may suggest claims become more severe rather than more frequent.
CC (Third-Party + Additional Coverages) remains relatively stable (0.59–0.66), indicating more consistent profitability across years.



Business Implication:

The simultaneous increase in both claim frequency and loss ratio suggests COMP_N may require closer monitoring, revised pricing strategies, stricter underwriting criteria, or refined risk segmentation approaches.
The increasing loss ratio observed in TP indicates that low claim occurrence does not necessarily imply low financial risk, highlighting the importance of evaluating both claim frequency and claim severity.
Products with relatively stable loss ratios, such as CC, may contribute greater predictability to portfolio profitability.
The observed differences demonstrate that insurance products exhibit heterogeneous risk characteristics and therefore may require differentiated pricing and portfolio management strategies.




5.3 Claim Frequency and Loss Ratio by Policy Activity Status
This analysis compares claim frequency and loss ratio between active and non-active policies across 2022–2024. The data was transformed into long format using pivot_longer() to enable simultaneous comparison of both performance metrics within a single visualisation.
Grouped bar charts were selected because they facilitate direct comparison between claim occurrence and underwriting profitability within each year and policy status category.

Coding Details

pivot_longer() reshapes claim frequency and loss ratio into a single metric column, making it easier to compare multiple performance indicators within one chart. recode() renames metric labels into more readable terms for presentation.
position_dodge() places bars and labels side-by-side instead of stacking them, allowing direct comparison between claim frequency and loss ratio across years.



ActiveNot Active




Show code
status_metrics_long <- status_year_metrics %>%
  mutate(claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure, loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium) %>%
  select(year, status_group, claim_frequency, loss_ratio) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(claim_frequency, loss_ratio), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(metric = recode(metric, "claim_frequency" = "Claim Frequency", "loss_ratio" = "Loss Ratio"))

ggplot(filter(status_metrics_long, status_group == "Active"), aes(x = factor(year), y = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .75), width = .65, color = "white", alpha = .9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), position = position_dodge(width = .75), vjust = -.3, size = 7, color = text_dark) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Claim Frequency" = primary_color, "Loss Ratio" = secondary_color)) +
  labs(title = "Claim Frequency and Loss Ratio for Active Policies", x = "Year", y = "Metric Value", fill = "Metric") +
  theme_va()













Show code
ggplot(filter(status_metrics_long, status_group == "Not Active"), aes(x = factor(year), y = value, fill = metric)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = .75), width = .65, color = "white", alpha = .9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), position = position_dodge(width = .75), vjust = -.3, size = 7, color = text_dark) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Claim Frequency" = primary_color, "Loss Ratio" = secondary_color)) +
  labs(title = "Claim Frequency and Loss Ratio for Not Active Policies", x = "Year", y = "Metric Value", fill = "Metric") +
  theme_va()













Observation

For active policies, claim frequency remains highly stable at approximately 0.29 across all years, suggesting relatively consistent claim occurrence among retained policyholders.
The loss ratio for active policies increases gradually from 0.60 (2022) to 0.69 (2024). Although remaining below 1, the upward trend indicates weakening underwriting profitability over time.
Not active policies exhibit substantially higher claim frequency (~0.49–0.51) compared to active policies, indicating claims occur more frequently within this segment.
The loss ratio for not active policies consistently exceeds 1.0, ranging between 1.23 and 1.37, suggesting incurred claims exceed collected premiums and indicating persistent underwriting losses.
The simultaneous presence of higher claim frequency and loss ratio among not active policies suggests this segment represents a higher-risk and less profitable group compared to active policies.



Business Implication:

The persistently elevated claim frequency and loss ratio observed among not active policies suggest these policies contribute disproportionately to portfolio risk and underwriting losses.
The findings may indicate that poorer claims experience is associated with increased policy cancellation or non-renewal behaviour, although further analysis is required to establish this relationship.
Investigating whether non-active policies share common characteristics, such as policy type, driver age, or vehicle profile, may support improved retention strategies and risk segmentation.
While active policies remain comparatively stable, the gradual increase in loss ratio suggests profitability should continue to be monitored over time.




5.4 Claims vs Incurred
A scatter plot with jitter was used to examine the relationship between total claims and total incurred amounts at the policy level.
The visualisation maps:

total_claims → x-axis (number of claims)
total_incurred → y-axis (total incurred claim cost)

Jittering (geom_jitter()) was applied to reduce overplotting because insurance data often contains repeated claim counts concentrated around similar values. A smoothed trend line (geom_smooth()) was included to highlight the overall relationship between claim occurrence and incurred cost.
Additionally, logarithmic transformations were applied to both axes (scale_x_log10() and scale_y_log10()) because claim costs are highly right-skewed. Without transformation, extreme claim values would dominate the visualisation and obscure patterns among lower-cost observations.

Coding Details

geom_jitter() adds random variation to point positions to reduce overlap, making dense observations easier to visualise. geom_smooth() overlays a trend line to show the overall relationship between total claims and incurred amounts.
scale_x_log10() and scale_y_log10() apply logarithmic scaling to both axes, improving visibility when values are highly skewed or span a wide range.



PlotCode














ggplot(
motor_clean,
aes(
x = total_claims + 1,
y = total_incurred + 1
)
)+
geom_jitter(
color = primary_color,
alpha = .15
)+
geom_smooth(
color = secondary_color,
se = FALSE
)+
scale_x_log10()+
scale_y_log10()+
labs(
title = "Claims vs Incurred (Log Scale)",
x = "Total Claims (log scale)", 
y = "Total Incurred (log scale)"
)+
theme_va()





Observation

The smoothed trend line indicates a positive relationship between claim count and incurred cost, suggesting policies with more claims generally generate higher losses.
The relationship is not strictly linear, as considerable variation in incurred amounts exists among policies with similar numbers of claims, particularly between 2 and 5 claims.
The substantial vertical dispersion suggests that claim severity differs considerably even when claim frequency is similar, indicating claim count alone does not fully explain incurred losses.
Several policies with relatively few claims exhibit exceptionally high incurred amounts, implying that infrequent but severe claims may contribute disproportionately to portfolio losses.
Multiple extreme outliers exceeding 100,000 monetary units are observed despite moderate claim counts, suggesting the presence of high-severity or catastrophic claim events.
The smoothed trend appears to flatten around 4–6 claims before increasing again, indicating increases in claim count do not always correspond proportionally to increases in incurred costs.



Business Implication:

The findings suggest that claim frequency alone is insufficient for evaluating portfolio risk, as claim severity introduces substantial variability in financial outcomes.
Policies associated with low-frequency but high-severity claims may generate significant underwriting risk despite relatively few claim events.
The presence of extreme incurred outliers suggests insurers may require targeted monitoring of high-severity segments, stronger underwriting controls, or reinsurance strategies to manage portfolio volatility.
Effective portfolio management should therefore consider both claim occurrence (frequency) and financial impact (severity) when assessing profitability and risk exposure.




5.5 Relationship Between Driver Age, Claim Frequency, and Loss Ratio
This animated visualisation examines how driver age distributions relate to claim frequency and loss ratio across selected policy types over time (2022–2024).
The analysis focuses on CC (Third-Party + Additional Coverages) and COMP_N (Comprehensive without Excess) to compare age-based risk patterns between a relatively stable product and a higher-risk segment identified in earlier analyses.
The visual combines:

Density curves (cloud) → distribution of policyholders by age
Rain/stem plots → mean risk metric (claim frequency or loss ratio) at each age
Animation (transition_states()) → temporal changes across years
Faceting → comparison across policy types and risk metrics

This layered approach allows simultaneous examination of demographic concentration, risk behaviour, and temporal evolution, which would be difficult to observe using static charts alone.
Extension:
The framework can be extended to other policy types (e.g., COMP_E, TP, TPG) by modifying the selected policy_type filter. This supports comparison of age-related risk patterns across different insurance products and enables broader portfolio segmentation analysis.
The animation cycles through yearly observations (2022–2024), allowing changes in age-related risk patterns to be observed over time.

Coding Details

is.finite() keeps only valid claim frequency and loss ratio values, removing infinite results that may occur from division issues. NA_real_ ensures missing numeric values are stored consistently as numeric NA.
geom_density() creates the driver age density “cloud”, while after_stat() rescales the density values so they fit visually within the plot. geom_segment() and geom_point() create the “rain” effect by showing scaled risk values below the age distribution.
facet_grid(metric ~ policy_type) separates the visualisation by metric and policy type, while transition_states() animates the chart across years.




Show code
risk_profile <- motor_clean %>%
  mutate(
    claim_frequency = if_else(
      total_exposure > 0,
      total_claims / total_exposure,
      NA_real_
    ),
    loss_ratio = if_else(
      total_premium > 0,
      total_incurred / total_premium,
      NA_real_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    policy_type %in% c("CC", "COMP_N"),
    !is.na(year),
    !is.na(driver_age),
    is.finite(claim_frequency),
    is.finite(loss_ratio)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    policy_type = recode(
      policy_type,
      "CC" = "Third-Party + Additional Coverages",
      "COMP_N" = "Comprehensive without Excess"
    )
  )

risk_metric <- risk_profile %>%
  group_by(year, policy_type, driver_age) %>%
  summarise(
    loss_ratio = mean(loss_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    claim_frequency = mean(claim_frequency, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(loss_ratio, claim_frequency),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  group_by(year, policy_type, metric) %>%
  mutate(
    value_scaled = value / max(value, na.rm = TRUE) * 1.2
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    metric = recode(
      metric,
      "loss_ratio" = "Loss Ratio",
      "claim_frequency" = "Claim Frequency"
    )
  )

ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    data = risk_profile,
    aes(
      x = driver_age,
      y = after_stat(density / max(density) * .8)
    ),
    fill = secondary_color,
    color = secondary_color,
    alpha = .65,
    adjust = 2
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    data = risk_metric,
    aes(
      x = driver_age,
      xend = driver_age,
      y = 0,
      yend = -value_scaled,
      color = metric
    ),
    alpha = .45,
    linewidth = .8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = risk_metric,
    aes(
      x = driver_age,
      y = -value_scaled,
      color = metric
    ),
    size = 2.2,
    alpha = .8
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Claim Frequency" = primary_color,
      "Loss Ratio" = fourth_color
    )
  ) +
  facet_grid(
    metric ~ policy_type
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(-1.35, .9),
    breaks = c(-1.2, 0, .8),
    labels = c("Higher Risk", "0", "Age Density")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age-Based Risk Profiles Across Selected Policy Types | Year: {closest_state}",
    subtitle = "Cloud = Driver age density | Rain = Mean risk metric by age",
    x = "Driver Age",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  transition_states(
    year,
    transition_length = 2,
    state_length = 5
  ) +
  theme_va() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )










Observation

Across all years, policyholders are primarily concentrated between approximately 35–65 years, indicating that middle-aged drivers dominate both selected policy categories.
COMP_N (Comprehensive without excess) consistently exhibits higher claim frequency and loss ratio across multiple age groups compared to CC, reinforcing earlier findings that COMP_N represents the highest-risk product segment.
Elevated risk metrics in COMP_N persist despite similar age concentration patterns, suggesting that policy characteristics may influence risk beyond demographic composition alone.
Risk metrics vary across ages, indicating that driver age does not have a uniform relationship with claim behaviour or profitability.
The animation suggests that risk profiles evolve over time, particularly within COMP_N, where higher claim frequency and loss ratios become more pronounced across later years.
The coexistence of dense middle-aged populations and elevated risk metrics implies that high-volume demographic groups may contribute disproportionately to portfolio performance outcomes.



Business Implication

The persistence of elevated risk metrics across age groups within COMP_N suggests that product design or underwriting conditions may influence portfolio risk beyond age effects alone.
Age-based segmentation may improve pricing precision, but demographic characteristics should be evaluated together with policy type to avoid oversimplified risk assessment.
Since middle-aged drivers represent the largest proportion of policyholders, changes in claims behaviour within this demographic may have substantial implications for overall portfolio profitability.
Animated temporal analysis highlights how risk patterns evolve over time, supporting proactive monitoring of emerging high-risk segments.

title: Take Home Exercise 1
text:
6 Summary and Future Research
Our analysis of the motor insurance portfolio examined relationships between policy types, demographics, retention behaviour, claim frequency, incurred losses, and underwriting profitability. Overall, the findings revealed substantial heterogeneity in risk and profitability across products and customer segments, suggesting portfolio performance is associated with multiple interacting factors rather than a single characteristic.

6.1 Key Findings:

The portfolio is highly concentrated in Third-Party + Additional Coverages (CC), indicating that overall portfolio performance may be disproportionately influenced by a small number of dominant products.
Policyholders are primarily concentrated within middle-aged groups (approximately 35–60 years), suggesting this demographic contributes substantially to portfolio exposure.
The proportion of inactive policies increases over time, potentially indicating weakening customer retention and increasing churn risk.
COMP_N (Comprehensive without excess) consistently demonstrates the highest claim frequency and loss ratio, exceeding a loss ratio of 1.0 in 2024. This suggests the segment may have transitioned into an underwriting loss position, making it the highest-risk and least profitable product within the portfolio.
In contrast, CC (Third-Party + Additional Coverages) maintains comparatively stable claim frequency and loss ratios, indicating more predictable underwriting performance.
Policies with relatively few claims may still generate substantial incurred costs, suggesting claim severity is an important determinant of portfolio volatility alongside claim frequency.
Not active policies exhibit both higher claim frequency and higher loss ratios compared to active policies, indicating these segments may contribute disproportionately to portfolio risk and underwriting losses.
Age-based analyses suggest that risk behaviour evolves over time and differs across policy types, highlighting potential interactions between demographic characteristics and product-specific risk exposure.

Collectively, the findings suggest that policy type, retention behaviour, claim frequency, and claim severity are associated with differences in portfolio risk, profitability, and volatility. Products exhibiting persistently elevated claim frequency and loss ratios appear more vulnerable to deteriorating underwriting performance, while severe but infrequent claims may contribute disproportionately to portfolio volatility.
However, as the current analysis is exploratory in nature, these relationships should be interpreted as associations rather than confirmed causal influences. Additional statistical testing is required to determine whether observed patterns represent significant drivers of profitability and risk.


6.2 Recommendations for Future Research

Confirmatory and Statistical Analysis
The current study identifies patterns and associations between portfolio characteristics and insurance performance but does not establish causal relationships. Future research should incorporate statistical hypothesis testing and confirmatory analysis to determine whether variables such as policy type, retention status, claim frequency, age, and claim severity significantly influence profitability and portfolio volatility.
Potential approaches include:

ANOVA / t-tests → compare profitability and claims metrics across policy groups
Chi-square tests → assess relationships between categorical variables
Correlation analysis → quantify strength of associations between portfolio characteristics and risk measures
Regression modelling → identify statistically significant predictors of claim frequency, loss ratio, or profitability
Survival analysis → investigate factors associated with customer retention and policy cancellation behaviour

These methods would provide stronger evidence regarding whether observed relationships represent true drivers of profitability and volatility rather than coincidental patterns.


Customer Retention and Churn Analysis
The increasing proportion of inactive policies suggests potential deterioration in customer retention over time. Future studies should investigate whether claim frequency, loss ratios, demographics, or policy characteristics are associated with policy cancellation or non-renewal behaviour.
Understanding these relationships may support improved customer retention strategies, pricing decisions, and long-term portfolio stability.


Claim Severity and Extreme Loss Analysis
While claim frequency explains how often claims occur, portfolio profitability may also be influenced by high-severity but infrequent claims. Further analysis of extreme incurred losses and outlier events could improve understanding of catastrophic risks and support decisions relating to:

pricing strategies,
underwriting controls,
reinsurance arrangements,
portfolio volatility management.



Advanced Risk Segmentation
Future research should examine interactions between variables such as:

driver age,
policy type,
retention status,
claim frequency,
claim severity,
profitability indicators.

Multivariate approaches may reveal complex risk segments not observable through pairwise comparisons and support more precise pricing and underwriting strategies.


Longitudinal Portfolio Monitoring
Extending analysis beyond the 2022–2024 period would enable evaluation of longer-term changes in:

portfolio composition,
profitability,
customer behaviour,
claims experience,
retention patterns.

Longitudinal studies may reveal structural shifts in risk behaviour and improve the insurer’s ability to anticipate emerging trends.


Incorporating Additional Risk Factors
Future analyses could incorporate variables including:

vehicle characteristics,
geographic factors,
driving behaviour,
usage patterns,
external economic conditions,

which may influence claims experience but were not explored within the current scope. Including these variables may provide a more comprehensive understanding of portfolio risk determinants.
By extending analysis towards confirmatory testing, predictive modelling, and deeper risk segmentation, future research may provide stronger evidence regarding the factors driving insurance profitability and volatility, thereby supporting more targeted underwriting strategies and sustainable portfolio management decisions.

Import Data

pop_data <- read_csv("data/respopagsex2000to2018_tidy.csv") 



Prepare the data

text:
Chapter 14: Heatmap for Visualising and Analysing Multivariate Data

Import data

wh <- read_csv("data/WHData-2018.csv")



Prepare data

# Convert tibble to data frame
wh_df <- as.data.frame(wh)

# Set row names using country names
row.names(wh_df) <- wh_df$Country

# Select variables
wh1 <- dplyr::select(wh_df, c(3, 7:12))

# Convert to matrix
wh_matrix <- data.matrix(wh1)



Static heatmap

The plotThe code



#|echo: false
#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale="column",
                      cexRow = 0.6, 
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))











#|eval: false
#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
wh_heatmap <- heatmap(wh_matrix,
                      scale="column",
                      cexRow = 0.6, 
                      cexCol = 0.8,
                      margins = c(10, 4))













Creating interactive heatmap

The plotThe code



#|echo: false
#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])








#|eval: false
#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)])










Data transformation

Scaling methodNormalising methodPercentising method



#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
heatmaply(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
          scale = "column")








#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))








#|fig-width: 12
#|fig-height: 8
heatmaply(percentize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]))










Clustering algotrithm
heatmaply supports a variety of hierarchical clustering algorithm. The main arguments provided are:

distfun: function used to compute the distance (dissimilarity) between both rows and columns. Defaults to dist. The options “pearson”, “spearman” and “kendall” can be used to use correlation-based clustering, which uses as.dist(1 - cor(t(x))) as the distance metric (using the specified correlation method).
hclustfun: function used to compute the hierarchical clustering when Rowv or Colv are not dendrograms. Defaults to hclust.
dist_method default is NULL, which results in “euclidean” to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to distfun. By default distfun is “dist”” hence this can be one of “euclidean”, “maximum”, “manhattan”, “canberra”, “binary” or “minkowski”.
hclust_method default is NULL, which results in “complete” method to be used. It can accept alternative character strings indicating the method to be passed to hclustfun. By default hclustfun is hclust hence this can be one of “ward.D”, “ward.D2”, “single”, “complete”, “average” (= UPGMA), “mcquitty” (= WPGMA), “median” (= WPGMC) or “centroid” (= UPGMC).

In general, a clustering model can be calibrated either manually or statistically.


Manual approach

heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "ward.D")







Statistical approach

wh_d <- dist(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]), method = "euclidean")
dend_expend(wh_d)[[3]]

  dist_methods hclust_methods     optim
1      unknown         ward.D 0.6765398
2      unknown        ward.D2 0.6700807
3      unknown         single 0.7219100
4      unknown       complete 0.7259444
5      unknown        average 0.8023959
6      unknown       mcquitty 0.7031276
7      unknown         median 0.7654802
8      unknown       centroid 0.8122677

wh_clust <- hclust(wh_d, method = "average")
num_k <- find_k(wh_clust)
plot(num_k)







heatmaply(normalize(wh_matrix[, -c(1, 2, 4, 5)]),
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          k_row = 3)







Seriation

title: Hands-on Exercise 5
text:
Chapter 16: Treemap Visualisation with R

Import data

realis2018 <- read_csv("data/realis2018.csv")

The data.frame realis2018 is in trasaction record form, which is highly disaggregated and not appropriate to be used to plot a treemap. In this section, we will perform the following steps to manipulate and prepare a data.frtame that is appropriate for treemap visualisation:

group transaction records by Project Name, Planning Region, Planning Area, Property Type and Type of Sale, and
compute Total Unit Sold, Total Area, Median Unit Price and Median Transacted Price by applying appropriate summary statistics on No. of Units, Area (sqm), Unit Price ($ psm) and Transacted Price ($) respectively.

Two key verbs of dplyr package, namely: group_by() and summarize() will be used to perform these steps.
group_by() breaks down a data.frame into specified groups of rows. When you then apply the verbs above on the resulting object they’ll be automatically applied “by group”.
Grouping affects the verbs as follows:

grouped select() is the same as ungrouped select(), except that grouping variables are always retained.
grouped arrange() is the same as ungrouped; unless you set .by_group = TRUE, in which case it orders first by the grouping variables.
mutate() and filter() are most useful in conjunction with window functions (like rank(), or min(x) == x). They are described in detail in vignette(“window-functions”).
sample_n() and sample_frac() sample the specified number/fraction of rows in each group.
summarise() computes the summary for each group.

In our case, group_by() will used together with summarise() to derive the summarised data.frame.


Data wrangling

Grouped summaries without the pipeGrouped summaries with the pipe



realis2018_grouped <- group_by(realis2018, `Project Name`,
                               `Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, 
                               `Property Type`, `Type of Sale`)
realis2018_summarised <- summarise(realis2018_grouped, 
                          `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
                          `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE), 
                          `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))




realis2018_summarised <- realis2018 %>% 
  group_by(`Project Name`,`Planning Region`, 
           `Planning Area`, `Property Type`, 
           `Type of Sale`) %>%
  summarise(`Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE), 
            `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
            `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE))






Design Treemap with treemap package


Design a static treemap

index

The index vector must consist of at least two column names or else no hierarchy treemap will be plotted.
If multiple column names are provided, such as the code chunk above, the first name is the highest aggregation level, the second name the second highest aggregation level, and so on.

vSize

The column must not contain negative values. This is because it’s vaues will be used to map the sizes of the rectangles of the treemaps.



The plotThe code














realis2018_selected <- realis2018_summarised %>%
  filter(`Property Type` == "Condominium", `Type of Sale` == "Resale")
treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type = "value",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )






Colors in treemap package

The “value” type treemapThe “manual”type treemap



treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="value",
        palette="RdYlBu", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )













Treemap layout

Working with algorithm argumentUsing sortID



treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "squarified",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )











treemap(realis2018_selected,
        index=c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
        vSize="Total Unit Sold",
        vColor="Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
        type="manual",
        palette="Blues", 
        algorithm = "pivotSize",
        sortID = "Median Transacted Price",
        title="Resale Condominium by Planning Region and Area, 2017",
        title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ per sq. m)"
        )
