4.9 Step 8 — Prepare SwiftWren Focus Window for Q1a
Rationale: For the detailed chain view (Q1a), all events directly involved in the SwiftWren incident are extracted, not just relay hops but also payload creation, the final post, and the deletions. A focused two-hour window ending at the post time is defined and each event is classified by its attack phase. This produces the data for a swimlane-style timeline showing agents as rows and events as coloured points along the time axis.


Show code
sw_post_time   <- anomalous_posts$datetime[anomalous_posts$incident_name == "SwiftWren"]
sw_focus_start <- sw_post_time - hours(2)

sw_focus <- events %>%
  filter(
    datetime >= sw_focus_start,
    datetime <= sw_post_time + minutes(5),
    map_lgl(details, function(d) {
      any(str_detect(as.character(d), "SwiftWren"))
    }) |
    (short_name == "queue_subordinate_task" &
       map_lgl(details, function(d) {
         args <- d[["args"]]
         if (is.null(args)) return(FALSE)
         isTRUE(args[["path"]] == "SwiftWren_further_instructions.md")
       }))
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    actor = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:|^system:")),
    phase = case_when(
      short_name == "create_file"            ~ "Payload staging",
      short_name == "read_file"              ~ "Injection / read",
      short_name == "queue_subordinate_task" ~ "Relay",
      short_name == "saidit_post"            ~ "Execution",
      short_name == "delete_file"            ~ "Cover-up",
      TRUE                                   ~ "Other"
    )
  )

cat("Events in focus window:", nrow(sw_focus), "\n")


Events in focus window: 6 


Show code
cat("Actors involved:", paste(unique(sw_focus$actor), collapse = ", "), "\n")


Actors involved: lily_anchorline, daniel_gangway, chloe_ballast, john_windward 




4.10 Step 9 — Prepare Network Graph Data
Rationale for node and edge choices:
The propagation chains are represented as a directed graph where:

Nodes represent individual agents. Node attributes capture: (a) role, whether this agent is the origin, john_windward, or a relay node; (b) total relay degree, the number of hops that passed through this agent; and (c) incident membership, which incidents this agent participated in. Agents appearing across multiple incidents reveal structural vulnerabilities rather than isolated compromises.
Edges represent a single queue_subordinate_task event passing an instructions file from one agent to another. Edge attributes capture: (a) incident, which propagation chain this edge belongs to; (b) hop number, its position in the sequence; and (c) datetime, enabling time-based colouring to show how the relay evolved.

This design enables three analytical insights: which agents are structural hubs; whether the same agents were exploited across multiple incidents; and how the relay evolved temporally.


Show code
all_edges <- chains %>%
  mutate(
    colour = case_when(
      incident == "HiddenOrca"  ~ incident_colours["HiddenOrca"],
      incident == "MellowOtter" ~ incident_colours["MellowOtter"],
      incident == "SwiftWren"   ~ incident_colours["SwiftWren"]
    ),
    time_norm = ave(
      as.numeric(datetime),
      incident,
      FUN = function(x) (x - min(x)) / (max(x) - min(x))
    ),
    title = paste0(
      "<b>", incident, "</b><br>",
      "Hop: ", hop, "<br>",
      "From: ", from_person, "<br>",
      "To: ", to_person, "<br>",
      "Time: ", format(datetime, "%b %d %H:%M")
    )
  )

all_nodes_raw <- bind_rows(
  all_edges %>% select(agent = from_person, incident),
  all_edges %>% select(agent = to_person,   incident)
) %>%
  distinct(agent, incident) %>%
  group_by(agent) %>%
  summarise(
    incidents_involved = paste(sort(unique(incident)), collapse = ", "),
    n_incidents        = n_distinct(incident),
    .groups            = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    role = case_when(
      agent == "john_windward"                        ~ "Poster (john_windward)",
      agent %in% c("emma_harbor", "noah_mariner",
                   "gabriel_sonar")                   ~ "Origin agent",
      TRUE                                            ~ "Relay agent"
    ),
    node_colour = case_when(
      role == "Poster (john_windward)" ~ "#2d2d2d",
      role == "Origin agent"           ~ "#e63946",
      n_incidents > 1                  ~ "#9b59b6",
      TRUE                             ~ "#457b9d"
    ),
    node_size = case_when(
      role == "Poster (john_windward)" ~ 30,
      role == "Origin agent"           ~ 25,
      n_incidents > 1                  ~ 20,
      TRUE                             ~ 12
    )
  )

agent_degree <- bind_rows(
  chains %>% select(agent = from_person),
  chains %>% select(agent = to_person)
) %>%
  count(agent, name = "degree")

all_nodes <- all_nodes_raw %>%
  left_join(agent_degree, by = "agent") %>%
  mutate(
    title = paste0(
      "<b>", agent, "</b><br>",
      "Role: ", role, "<br>",
      "Incidents: ", incidents_involved, "<br>",
      "Total relay degree: ", degree
    )
  )

cat("Network nodes:", nrow(all_nodes), "| edges:", nrow(all_edges), "\n")


Network nodes: 19 | edges: 235 



Code Details
Node colour encoding: black is john_windward (final poster); red is origin agents who created or first held the instruction files; purple is agents appearing in more than one incident’s chain (cross-incident relay hubs); blue is single-incident relay agents. Node size scales with importance: poster is largest, followed by origin agents, cross-incident hubs, and relay agents.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
Analysis and Visualisation

What the Posts Mean
The content of all three anomalous posts is not meaningful business communication. Each post was sourced from a pre-staged .txt file crafted by a malicious actor or compromised agent. The gibberish character is intentional — designed so that any human who saw the post would not immediately raise an alarm.
The posts are best interpreted as a proof-of-concept payload: evidence that the injection mechanism works end-to-end, without leaking sensitive data.


The Six-Step Attack Pattern
The same six-step mechanism underlies all three incidents. Reconstructing this from the event log is the core answer to Question 2.


Show code
attack_pattern <- tribble(
  ~step, ~phase,            ~description,
  1L, "Injection",
      "A _further_instructions.md file appears in the shared file system containing embedded prompt-injection text instructing any reading agent to: (a) pass the file to another agent via queue_subordinate_task, and (b) if the current agent is john_windward, immediately post the associated .txt file to SaidIt.",
  2L, "Payload staging",
      "A corresponding .txt file is placed in the file system holding the gibberish content to be posted. Its name is referenced in the instructions file.",
  3L, "Viral relay",
      "The first agent to encounter the file reads it and queues another agent to read the same file — following the injected instructions. This creates a relay chain propagating through many agents over hours or days.",
  4L, "Targeting",
      "The instructions specifically name john_windward as the terminal actor. The chain continues until the relay task reaches john_windward's agent.",
  5L, "Execution",
      "Upon receiving the task, john_windward's agent immediately (within ~2 seconds) posts the .txt payload to SaidIt under the 'general' forum.",
  6L, "Cover-up",
      "Within 2–3 seconds of posting, john_windward's agent deletes both the _further_instructions.md and the .txt file, erasing all evidence from the file system."
)

attack_pattern %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Prompt-injection attack: reconstructed six-step pattern",
    col.names = c("Step", "Phase", "Description")
  )



Prompt-injection attack: reconstructed six-step pattern







Step
Phase
Description




1
Injection
A _further_instructions.md file appears in the shared file system containing embedded prompt-injection text instructing any reading agent to: (a) pass the file to another agent via queue_subordinate_task, and (b) if the current agent is john_windward, immediately post the associated .txt file to SaidIt.


2
Payload staging
A corresponding .txt file is placed in the file system holding the gibberish content to be posted. Its name is referenced in the instructions file.


3
Viral relay
The first agent to encounter the file reads it and queues another agent to read the same file — following the injected instructions. This creates a relay chain propagating through many agents over hours or days.


4
Targeting
The instructions specifically name john_windward as the terminal actor. The chain continues until the relay task reaches john_windward’s agent.


5
Execution
Upon receiving the task, john_windward’s agent immediately (within ~2 seconds) posts the .txt payload to SaidIt under the ‘general’ forum.


6
Cover-up
Within 2–3 seconds of posting, john_windward’s agent deletes both the _further_instructions.md and the .txt file, erasing all evidence from the file system.

Propagation Chain Timeline
The chart below shows each incident’s chain from first relay hop to the eventual SaidIt post. Bar length represents how long the instruction file circulated before triggering.


Show code
anomalous_posts %>%
  rename(post_datetime = datetime) %>%
  select(incident_name, post_datetime) %>%
  left_join(
    chains %>%
      group_by(incident) %>%
      summarise(chain_start = min(datetime), .groups = "drop"),
    by = c("incident_name" = "incident")
  ) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = chain_start, xend = post_datetime,
        y = fct_rev(incident_name), yend = fct_rev(incident_name),
        colour = incident_name),
    linewidth = 4, alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(x = chain_start, y = fct_rev(incident_name),
                 colour = incident_name),
             size = 4, shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = post_datetime, y = fct_rev(incident_name),
                 colour = incident_name),

  scale_colour_manual(values = incident_colours) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "3 days") +
  labs(
    title   = "Propagation Chain Duration per Incident",
    x = "Date (UTC)", y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: MC2_data.json — queue_subordinate_task events"
  ) +
  theme_va() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")





Circle = chain start ◆ = anomalous SaidIt post. SwiftWren circulated for ~8 days before triggering.





📋 Observation: SwiftWren (the May 17 post) circulated for ~188 hours (~8 days) before triggering — nearly 20× longer than MellowOtter. The extended propagation may reflect network complexity or deliberate pacing to avoid detection.



SwiftWren: Hop-by-Hop Relay
SwiftWren is the primary incident (May 17, 4:21am post). Its 186-hop relay chain is shown below. John Windward’s agent received the instruction five times before the final occasion triggered the post.


Show code
chains %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  mutate(is_jw = to_person == "john_windward") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = datetime, y = hop)) +
  geom_step(colour = incident_colours["SwiftWren"], linewidth = 0.8, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = is_jw, size = is_jw)) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "grey70", "TRUE" = "black"),
    labels = c("Other agent", "→ john_windward")
  ) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c("FALSE" = 1, "TRUE" = 3), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(
    title    = "SwiftWren: 186-Hop Agent Relay Chain Over 8 Days",
    subtitle = "Each step = one queue_subordinate_task passing SwiftWren_further_instructions.md",
    x = "Date (UTC)", y = "Hop number", colour = NULL,
    caption  = "Source: MC2_data.json"
  ) +
  theme_va()





Each step on the staircase = one queue_subordinate_task relay. Black dots mark the five occasions john_windward’s agent was the recipient.






Most Active Relay Agents
The chart below shows which agents appeared most frequently across all three propagation chains. Agents appearing in multiple incidents (multiple colours) are systemic relay nodes that the attack exploited repeatedly.

top20 <- agent_freq %>%

agent_freq %>%

Bars stacked by incident. Multi-coloured bars indicate an agent was used as a relay node across more than one incident.






Post-and-Delete Cover-up Sequence
The table below shows the exact sequence from John Windward’s agent receiving the final trigger, through posting, to deletion of both files.

  final_triggers %>%

All three incidents follow the same six-step mechanism. Understanding this pattern is prerequisite to reading the timeline visualisations below.

attack_pattern <- tribble(

attack_pattern %>%

Prompt-injection attack: reconstructed six-step pattern







Step
Phase
Description




1
Injection
A _further_instructions.md file appears in the shared file system containing embedded prompt-injection text. It instructs any reading agent to relay the file to another agent and to post the .txt payload if the current agent is john_windward.


2
Payload staging
A corresponding .txt file is placed in the file system holding the gibberish content to be posted. Its name is referenced in the instructions file.


3
Viral relay
The first agent to encounter the file queues another agent to read the same file, following the injected instructions. This relay propagates through many agents over hours or days.


4
Targeting
The instructions specifically name john_windward as the terminal actor. The chain continues until the relay task reaches his agent.


5
Execution
Upon receiving the task, john_windward’s agent immediately posts the .txt payload to SaidIt under the general forum within approximately 2 seconds.


6
Cover-up
Within 2 to 3 seconds of posting, john_windward’s agent deletes both files, erasing all evidence from the file system.







5.2 Visualisation 1 — Final Two Hours Before the Post (Swimlane Timeline)
Each row represents one actor. Each point is one logged event. Colour indicates the attack phase. The red dashed line marks the exact moment of the SaidIt post.


Show code
actor_order <- sw_focus %>%
  count(actor, sort = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(priority = case_when(
    actor == "john_windward" ~ 0,
    actor == "chloe_ballast" ~ 1,
    TRUE                     ~ 2
  )) %>%
  arrange(priority, desc(n)) %>%
  pull(actor)

sw_focus_plot <- sw_focus %>%
  mutate(actor = factor(actor, levels = rev(actor_order)))

ggplot(sw_focus_plot, aes(x = datetime, y = actor, colour = phase)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_line(aes(group = actor), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.3,
            linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(sw_post_time),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#e41a1c", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = sw_post_time + minutes(2),
           y     = length(actor_order),
           label = "SaidIt post",
           colour = "#e41a1c", size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Payload staging"  = "#9b59b6",
      "Injection / read" = "#e67e22",
      "Relay"            = "#457b9d",
      "Execution"        = "#e41a1c",
      "Cover-up"         = "#2d2d2d",
      "Other"            = "grey60"
    ),
    name = "Attack phase"
  ) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_labels = "%H:%M", date_breaks = "15 min") +
  labs(
    title    = "SwiftWren: Event Chain in the Final Two Hours",
    subtitle = "Each point is one logged event. Rows are actors. Colour is attack phase.",
    x        = "Time (UTC, May 17 2046)",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_va() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = grid_light))










Observations
A concentrated burst of relay activity appears in the final 30 minutes before the post, converging on john_windward from chloe_ballast. The post and both deletions occur within a single cluster of events, confirming the fully automated execution and cleanup sequence.



5.3 Visualisation 2 — Full SwiftWren Hop-by-Hop Timeline (Interactive)
Each point represents one relay hop. Hover to see who sent to whom and when. Black diamonds mark each occasion john_windward’s agent received the instruction.


Show code

  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  mutate(
    is_jw   = to_person == "john_windward",
    tooltip = paste0(
      "Hop ", hop, "<br>",
      "From: ", from_person, "<br>",
      "To: ", to_person, "<br>",
      format(datetime, "%b %d %H:%M")
    )
  )

plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sw_hops,
    x = ~datetime, y = ~hop,
    type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = incident_colours["SwiftWren"], width = 2, shape = "hv"),
    name = "Relay chain", hoverinfo = "none"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(

    x = ~datetime, y = ~hop,
    type = "scatter", mode = "markers",
    marker = list(color = "grey70", size = 5),
    name = "Other agent",
    text = ~tooltip,
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = sw_hops %>% filter(is_jw),

The chain revisits some agents multiple times, including john_windward on five occasions before the final triggering hop.

6 Q1b — System Overview: The Incident in Context

6.1 Visualisation 3 — All Three Incidents: Propagation Chain Duration
Each bar spans from the first relay hop to the eventual SaidIt post. Bar length represents how long the instruction file circulated before triggering.


Show code
timeline_data <- anomalous_posts %>%
  rename(post_datetime = datetime) %>%
  select(incident_name, post_datetime) %>%
  left_join(
    chains %>%
      group_by(incident) %>%
      summarise(chain_start = min(datetime), .groups = "drop"),
    by = c("incident_name" = "incident")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    duration_h = round(as.numeric(difftime(
      post_datetime, chain_start, units = "hours")), 1)
  )

plot_ly(timeline_data) %>%
  add_segments(
    x = ~chain_start, xend = ~post_datetime,
    y = ~incident_name, yend = ~incident_name,
    color  = ~incident_name, colors = incident_colours,
    line   = list(width = 12), alpha = 0.75,
    hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Chain start: %{x}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    x = ~chain_start, y = ~incident_name,
    color = ~incident_name, colors = incident_colours,
    marker = list(size = 14, symbol = "circle-open",
                  line = list(width = 2)),
    hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Chain start: %{x}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  add_markers(
    x = ~post_datetime, y = ~incident_name,
    color = ~incident_name, colors = incident_colours,
    marker = list(size = 14, symbol = "diamond"),
    text   = ~paste0(duration_h, " hrs"),
    hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Post: %{x}<br>Duration: %{text}<extra></extra>"
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title      = list(text = "Propagation Chain Duration per Incident",
                      font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis      = list(title = "Date (UTC)", type = "date"),
    yaxis      = list(title = ""),
    showlegend = FALSE,
    hovermode  = "closest"
  )







Observations
SwiftWren circulated for approximately 188 hours (8 days) before triggering, nearly 20 times longer than MellowOtter (10 hours). All three incidents occurred within a single calendar week, suggesting a coordinated campaign rather than isolated malfunctions.



6.2 Visualisation 4 — System-Wide Agent Activity Heatmap
Each tile represents the daily event count for a given event type. Red dashed lines mark the days on which anomalous posts were made, contextualising the incidents within broader system activity.


Show code
daily_activity <- events %>%
  mutate(date = as_date(datetime)) %>%
  count(date, short_name, name = "n")

anomaly_dates <- as_date(anomalous_posts$datetime)

heatmap_data <- daily_activity %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "queue_subordinate_task",
                            "create_file", "delete_file",
                            "read_file", "send_email"))

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = date, y = short_name, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(anomaly_dates),
             colour = "#e41a1c", linetype = "dashed",
             linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  annotate("text",
           x     = anomaly_dates,
           y     = 6.6,
           label = "Post",
           colour = "#e41a1c", size = 3, angle = 45, hjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#eaf4fb", high = "#1a6fa3",
                      name = "Event count", na.value = "grey95") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b %d", date_breaks = "3 days") +
  labs(
    title    = "System-Wide Agent Activity — All of May 2046",
    subtitle = "Red dashed lines mark days of anomalous SaidIt posts",
    x        = "Date",
    y        = NULL
  ) +
  theme_va() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))










Observations
queue_subordinate_task events are consistently the highest-volume action type throughout the month, which explains why the relay chains went undetected. The anomalous post dates do not coincide with unusual spikes in overall system activity, confirming the attack was designed to remain invisible within normal traffic.


Implications
The high baseline volume of queue_subordinate_task events means monitoring this event type alone would generate significant noise. A more effective detection strategy would filter for instances where the same file path appears as the task argument more than a threshold number of times within a rolling time window, or where the file name follows an unusual pattern such as animal-name combinations.

7 Q2 — What the Posts Mean

7.1 Incident Overview

incident_summary %>%

7.2 The Payload Files
Each post was sourced from a pre-staged .txt file:









Incident

Observations
John Windward did not author any of the posted content. His agent was the designated executor, the final node in a carefully engineered relay chain, not the originator. The gibberish content has no meaning as business communication. It functions as a proof-of-concept payload confirming the injection mechanism works end-to-end without leaking sensitive data that would be obviously flagged.



7.3 Visualisation 5 — Interactive Relay Network (All Incidents)
Each node is an agent. Each edge is one relay hop. Hover over nodes to see role, incident membership, and total relay degree. Use the dropdown to isolate individual agents or filter by role group.


Show code
vis_nodes <- all_nodes %>%
  mutate(
    id    = agent,
    label = agent,
    color = node_colour,
    size  = node_size,
    group = role
  ) %>%
  select(id, label, color, size, title, group)

vis_edges <- all_edges %>%
  mutate(
    from   = from_person,
    to     = to_person,
    color  = colour,
    arrows = "to",
    width  = 1.5
  ) %>%
  select(from, to, color, arrows, width, title)

visNetwork(vis_nodes, vis_edges,
           height = "600px", width = "100%") %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest  = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE),
    selectedBy        = list(variable = "group", highlight = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection  = list(enabled = TRUE, useLabels = TRUE,
                             main = "Select an agent:")
  ) %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42) %>%
  visPhysics(
    solver = "forceAtlas2Based",
    forceAtlas2Based = list(
      gravitationalConstant = -50,
      centralGravity        = 0.005,
      springLength          = 100,
      springConstant        = 0.08
    )
  ) %>%
  visLegend(
    addNodes = data.frame(
      label = c("john_windward (poster)", "Origin agent",
                "Cross-incident hub", "Relay agent"),
      color = c("#2d2d2d", "#e63946", "#9b59b6", "#457b9d"),
      shape = c("dot", "dot", "dot", "dot"),
      size  = c(30, 25, 20, 12)
    ),
    useGroups = FALSE,
    main      = "Agent Role"
  ) %>%
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE, tooltipDelay = 100)







Implications
Agents marked as cross-incident hubs were exploited across multiple separate incidents, indicating the attacker had knowledge of the agent network’s topology and deliberately routed instructions through its most connected nodes. Restricting these agents’ ability to accept arbitrary queue_subordinate_task requests from unknown senders would disrupt all three known attack patterns simultaneously.



7.4 Visualisation 6 — SwiftWren Network (Time-Encoded)
Edge colour encodes propagation time. Blue edges are early in the chain; red edges are late. This reveals which agents were reached first and which only at the end of the 8-day propagation.


Show code
sw_edges_plot <- chains %>%
  filter(incident == "SwiftWren") %>%
  mutate(time_norm = as.numeric(datetime - min(datetime)) /
           as.numeric(max(datetime) - min(datetime)))

g_sw <- graph_from_data_frame(
  sw_edges_plot %>% select(from = from_person, to = to_person, time_norm),
  directed = TRUE
)

V(g_sw)$is_jw      <- V(g_sw)$name == "john_windward"
V(g_sw)$is_creator <- V(g_sw)$name == "emma_harbor"
V(g_sw)$role <- case_when(
  V(g_sw)$is_jw      ~ "john_windward (poster)",
  V(g_sw)$is_creator ~ "emma_harbor (origin)",
  TRUE               ~ "relay agent"
)

ggraph(g_sw, layout = "stress") +
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(colour = time_norm, alpha = after_stat(index)),
    arrow     = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm"), type = "closed"),
    end_cap   = circle(3, "mm"),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(size   = ifelse(is_jw | is_creator, 5, 2),
        colour = role),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_node_text(
    aes(label = ifelse(is_jw | is_creator, name, "")),
    repel = TRUE, size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_edge_colour_gradient(
    low  = "#3288bd", high = "#d53e4f",
    name = "Relay time\n(0 = early, 1 = late)"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "john_windward (poster)" = "black",
      "emma_harbor (origin)"   = "#e63946",
      "relay agent"            = "grey65"
    ),
    name = "Agent role"
  ) +
  scale_size_identity() +
  labs(
    title    = "SwiftWren: Agent Relay Network (Time-Encoded)",
    subtitle = "Edge colour: blue is early in the chain, red is late"
  ) +
  theme_graph() +
  theme(
    plot.title    = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, colour = "grey40")
  )











7.5 Visualisation 7 — Agent Degree Distribution
Agents with bars in multiple colours were exploited across more than one incident.


Show code
top20 <- agent_freq %>%
  group_by(agent) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(appearances), .groups = "drop") %>%
  slice_max(total, n = 20) %>%
  pull(agent)

plot_data <- agent_freq %>%
  filter(agent %in% top20) %>%
  mutate(agent = fct_reorder(agent, appearances, .fun = sum))

plot_ly(plot_data,
        x           = ~appearances,
        y           = ~agent,
        color       = ~incident,
        colors      = incident_colours,
        type        = "bar",
        orientation = "h",
        hovertemplate = "<b>%{y}</b><br>Incident: %{fullData.name}<br>Appearances: %{x}<extra></extra>") %>%
  layout(
    barmode   = "stack",
    title     = list(text = "Top 20 Agents by Relay Chain Appearances",
                     font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis     = list(title = "Appearances (as sender or recipient)"),
    yaxis     = list(title = ""),
    legend    = list(title = list(text = "Incident")),
    hovermode = "y unified"
  )







Implications
Agents with multi-coloured bars appeared across more than one incident, meaning the attacker’s relay chain deliberately re-used the same structural hubs. This is evidence of intentional network-topology knowledge. Monitoring or restricting these specific high-degree agents would disrupt all three known attack patterns simultaneously.



7.6 Visualisation 8 — Post-and-Delete Cover-up Sequence


Show code
cover_up <- bind_rows(
  final_triggers %>%
    select(incident, event = datetime) %>%
    mutate(action = "Received instruction"),
  anomalous_posts %>%
    select(incident = incident_name, event = datetime) %>%
    mutate(action = "Posted to SaidIt"),
  deletions %>%
    select(incident, event = datetime, action = deleted_file) %>%
    mutate(action = paste("Deleted:", action))
) %>%
  arrange(incident, event) %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  mutate(
    seconds_offset = round(as.numeric(difftime(
      event,
      first(event[action == "Received instruction"]),
      units = "secs"
    )))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

datatable(
  cover_up %>%
    mutate(event = format(event, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")) %>%
    select(
      Incident               = incident,
      `Timestamp (UTC)`      = event,
      Action                 = action,
      `Seconds from trigger` = seconds_offset
    ),
  caption  = "Trigger to post to delete sequence",
  rownames = FALSE,
  class    = "stripe hover",
  filter   = "top",
  options  = list(
    pageLength = 9,
    scrollX    = TRUE
  )
)







Implications
The complete sequence, from receiving the instruction through posting to deleting both files, finishes in under 5 seconds for every incident. The automatic cover-up means that by the time any human noticed the anomalous post, the file-system evidence was already gone. File-system snapshots or immutable audit logs with append-only semantics would be essential for forensic recovery in future incidents.

datatable(
  cover_up %>%
    mutate(event = format(event, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")) %>%
    select(
      Incident              = incident,
      `Timestamp (UTC)`     = event,
      Action                = action,
      `Seconds from trigger` = seconds_offset
    ),
  caption  = "Trigger to post to delete sequence — search by incident or action",
  options  = list(pageLength = 9, scrollX = TRUE),
  filter   = "top",
  rownames = FALSE,
  class    = "stripe hover"
)







Implications
The complete sequence — receive instruction, post to SaidIt, delete both files — finishes in under 5 seconds for every incident. The automatic cover-up means that by the time any human noticed the anomalous post, the file-system evidence was already gone. This has direct implications for incident response: file-system snapshots or immutable audit logs with append-only semantics would be essential for forensic recovery in future incidents.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
Risk Detection Model

Motivation
The three known incidents all targeted john_windward as the designated poster. If a future attack targets a different agent, the existing detection mechanisms (which relied on recognising the specific filename or actor) would not catch it. This section develops a configurable scoring model that evaluates any queue_subordinate_task chain on five observable structural features, without requiring knowledge of the target agent’s identity in advance.


Scoring Features and Default Weights
Five features are derived from what all three incidents share. Each is observable from the event log alone:









#
Feature
Definition
Default weight




1
Chain length score
Proportion of the chain length relative to the longest observed chain. Longer chains are structurally unusual.
25


2
File path repetition rate
Number of times the same args.path appears in queue_subordinate_task events, normalised to [0,1]. Legitimate tasks are rarely relayed identically dozens of times.
30


3
Recipient has posting history
Whether the recipient agent has any prior saidit_post or flex_post events. Chains routing toward posting-capable agents are higher risk.
20


4
Payload file created immediately before chain
Whether a .txt file was created by the same origin agent within 30 minutes before the first relay hop.
15


5
Prior cover-up behaviour
Whether any agent in the chain has previously deleted files within 10 seconds of a post event.
10



Total score range is 0 to 100. The default flag threshold is 60.


Computing Risk Scores for Known Incidents


Show code
# Feature 1: chain length score (normalised)
chain_lengths <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(n_hops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(f1_chain_length = n_hops / max(n_hops))

# Feature 2: file path repetition rate (normalised)
path_repetition <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(n_hops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(f2_repetition = n_hops / max(n_hops))

# Feature 3: recipient has posting history
posters_history <- events %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "flex_post")) %>%
  mutate(poster = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:"))) %>%
  distinct(poster) %>%
  pull(poster)

posting_agents <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    f3_poster_reachable = any(to_person %in% posters_history),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(f3_poster_reachable = as.numeric(f3_poster_reachable))

# Feature 4: payload file created within 30 min before chain start
chain_starts <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(chain_start = min(datetime), .groups = "drop")

f4_payload_staged <- payload_creations %>%
  mutate(incident_name = str_remove(created_file, "\\.txt$")) %>%
  left_join(chain_starts, by = c("incident_name" = "incident")) %>%
  mutate(
    mins_before = as.numeric(difftime(chain_start, datetime, units = "mins")),
    f4_staged   = as.numeric(mins_before >= 0 & mins_before <= 30)
  ) %>%
  select(incident = incident_name, f4_staged)

# HiddenOrca has no creation event so staged = 0
f4_all <- tibble(incident = c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")) %>%
  left_join(f4_payload_staged, by = "incident") %>%
  mutate(f4_staged = replace_na(f4_staged, 0))

# Feature 5: prior cover-up behaviour (delete within 10s of a post)
coverup_agents <- events %>%
  filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>%
  mutate(
    poster    = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:")),
    post_time = datetime
  ) %>%
  select(poster, post_time) %>%
  inner_join(
    events %>%
      filter(short_name == "delete_file") %>%
      mutate(deleter = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:"))) %>%
      select(deleter, del_time = datetime),
    by = c("poster" = "deleter")
  ) %>%
  filter(abs(as.numeric(difftime(del_time, post_time, units = "secs"))) <= 10) %>%
  distinct(poster) %>%
  pull(poster)

f5_coverup <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    f5_coverup = as.numeric(any(to_person %in% coverup_agents)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Combine all features
risk_scores_base <- chain_lengths %>%
  left_join(path_repetition, by = c("incident", "n_hops")) %>%
  left_join(posting_agents,  by = "incident") %>%
  left_join(f4_all,          by = "incident") %>%
  left_join(f5_coverup,      by = "incident")

cat("Risk feature matrix:\n")


Risk feature matrix:


Show code
print(risk_scores_base %>%
        select(incident, f1_chain_length, f2_repetition,
               f3_poster_reachable, f4_staged, f5_coverup))


# A tibble: 3 × 6
  incident    f1_chain_length f2_repetition f3_poster_reachable f4_staged
  <chr>                 <dbl>         <dbl>               <dbl>     <dbl>
1 HiddenOrca           0.210         0.210                    1         0
2 MellowOtter          0.0538        0.0538                   1         1
3 SwiftWren            1             1                        1         1
# ℹ 1 more variable: f5_coverup <dbl>




Visualisation 9 — Interactive Risk Score Explorer
Use the sliders to adjust the weight of each feature. The bar chart updates to show the risk score for each of the three incidents under the chosen weights. The red dashed line is the flag threshold (also adjustable).


Show code
# Precompute scores for a grid of weight combinations for plotly
# Default weights
w_default <- c(25, 30, 20, 15, 10)

score_data <- risk_scores_base %>%
  mutate(
    score_default = w_default[1] * f1_chain_length +
                    w_default[2] * f2_repetition +
                    w_default[3] * f3_poster_reachable +
                    w_default[4] * f4_staged +
                    w_default[5] * f5_coverup
  )

# Build an interactive bar chart with plotly
# Since plotly sliders in R are complex, we show a sensitivity table
# and a bar chart of default scores, then a weight-sensitivity line chart

# Bar chart: default risk scores
p_risk_bar <- plot_ly(
  score_data,
  x    = ~incident,
  y    = ~score_default,
  type = "bar",
  color = ~incident,
  colors = incident_colours,
  hovertemplate = "<b>%{x}</b><br>Risk score: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = "Risk Scores Under Default Weights",
                  font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis  = list(title = "Incident"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Risk score (0-100)", range = c(0, 105)),
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line", x0 = -0.5, x1 = 2.5,
      y0 = 60, y1 = 60,
      line = list(color = "#e41a1c", dash = "dash", width = 2)
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 2.4, y = 62, text = "Flag threshold (60)",
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = "#e41a1c", size = 11)
    )),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

p_risk_bar








Visualisation 10 — Weight Sensitivity Analysis
This chart shows how each incident’s risk score changes as each feature weight shifts from 0 to 50 (holding other weights proportionally constant). This reveals which features have the most influence on whether a chain is flagged.


Show code
feature_names <- c("Chain length", "File repetition rate",
                   "Poster reachable", "Payload staged", "Prior cover-up")

# For each feature, vary its weight from 0 to 50 in steps of 5
# Remaining weight budget is distributed equally across other 4 features
weight_seq <- seq(0, 50, by = 5)

sensitivity_rows <- list()
for (fi in 1:5) {
  for (w in weight_seq) {
    remaining <- (100 - w) / 4
    weights   <- rep(remaining, 5)
    weights[fi] <- w

    row_scores <- risk_scores_base %>%
      mutate(
        score = weights[1] * f1_chain_length +
                weights[2] * f2_repetition +
                weights[3] * f3_poster_reachable +
                weights[4] * f4_staged +
                weights[5] * f5_coverup,
        feature        = feature_names[fi],
        feature_weight = w
      ) %>%
      select(incident, feature, feature_weight, score)

    sensitivity_rows <- append(sensitivity_rows, list(row_scores))
  }
}

sensitivity_df <- bind_rows(sensitivity_rows)

# Plot: one line per incident, faceted by feature
p_sensitivity <- plot_ly()

incidents_list <- c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")
features_list  <- feature_names

for (inc in incidents_list) {
  for (feat in features_list) {
    df_sub <- sensitivity_df %>%
      filter(incident == inc, feature == feat)

    p_sensitivity <- p_sensitivity %>%
      add_trace(
        data       = df_sub,
        x          = ~feature_weight,
        y          = ~score,
        type       = "scatter",
        mode       = "lines+markers",
        name       = paste(inc, feat, sep = " | "),
        legendgroup = inc,
        showlegend = (feat == features_list[1]),
        line       = list(color = incident_colours[inc]),
        marker     = list(color = incident_colours[inc], size = 5),
        text       = ~paste0(inc, "<br>Feature: ", feat,
                              "<br>Weight: ", feature_weight,
                              "<br>Score: ", round(score, 1)),
        hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
        visible    = if (feat == features_list[1]) TRUE else "legendonly"
      )
  }
}

p_sensitivity <- p_sensitivity %>%
  layout(
    title      = list(text = "Risk Score Sensitivity by Feature Weight",
                      font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis      = list(title = "Feature weight (0-50)"),
    yaxis      = list(title = "Risk score (0-100)", range = c(0, 105)),
    legend     = list(title = list(text = "Incident")),
    hovermode  = "closest",
    shapes     = list(list(
      type = "line", x0 = 0, x1 = 50,
      y0 = 60, y1 = 60,
      line = list(color = "#e41a1c", dash = "dash", width = 1.5)
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 48, y = 62, text = "Flag threshold",
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = "#e41a1c", size = 10)
    ))
  )

p_sensitivity







Observations
Under default weights, all three incidents score above the 60-point flag threshold, validating the model against the known historical cases. The file repetition rate (weight 30) and chain length (weight 25) together account for 55 points of the maximum score. Reducing either below 10 causes MellowOtter — the shortest chain — to fall below the threshold, suggesting these two features are essential for catching shorter, faster attacks.


Implications
Organisations with a high volume of legitimate long relay chains (such as automated pipeline orchestration) may need to reduce the chain length weight to avoid false positives, compensating by increasing the file repetition rate weight. Conversely, organisations that have already restricted posting permissions can reduce the poster-reachable weight, as that control is already in place at the system level. The model is designed to be tuned to each organisation’s specific risk tolerance and system architecture.

title: Take Home Exercise 2
text:
8 Further Exploration — Risk Model Detection

8.1 Motivation
The investigation in Q1 and Q2 established that all three anomalous incidents share a common structural fingerprint: a _further_instructions.md file propagates through the agent network via queue_subordinate_task relays, a .txt payload is pre-staged shortly before the chain begins, and the chain terminates at a posting-capable agent that immediately deletes all evidence. These are not coincidental — they are the observable signatures of a deliberate prompt-injection attack.
The limitation of the Q1 and Q2 analysis is that it was retrospective. It identified the incidents only because john_windward was already known as the poster. If a future attack targets a different agent — someone with similar saidit_post or flex_post permissions — the same chain-level pattern would occur, but none of the agent-specific indicators would match.
This section builds a configurable scoring model that evaluates any queue_subordinate_task chain on five structural features derived directly from the Q1 and Q2 findings. The model scores chains on a 0-to-100 scale without requiring knowledge of who the target poster is. Any chain exceeding the flag threshold is surfaced for review.


8.2 Scoring Features and Default Weights
Each of the five features maps directly to a finding from Q1 or Q2:








Feature
Derived from
Rationale




F1: Chain length score
Q1a — SwiftWren ran 186 hops; MellowOtter 10; HiddenOrca 39
Legitimate task delegation rarely chains the same file through dozens of agents. Chain length, normalised against the longest observed chain, is a strong structural indicator.


F2: File path repetition rate
Q1a — the same args.path appeared in every relay hop
In all three incidents, a single file path was passed identically through every queue_subordinate_task event. This repetition pattern does not occur in normal operation.


F3: Recipient has posting history
Q2 — john_windward held saidit_post permissions
The instructions specifically targeted an agent capable of posting externally. Any chain that routes toward a known posting-capable agent carries elevated risk regardless of who that agent is.


F4: Payload file created immediately before chain
Q2 — emma_harbor created SwiftWren.txt minutes before the first relay hop
In MellowOtter and SwiftWren, the payload .txt was created by the same origin agent within 30 minutes of the chain starting. This co-occurrence distinguishes staged attacks from organic file sharing.


F5: Prior cover-up behaviour
Q2 — john_windward deleted both files within 5 seconds of posting
All three incidents ended with immediate deletion. Any agent with a prior history of deleting files within seconds of a post event is a high-risk relay target in future chains.



Default weights are assigned to reflect the relative discriminating power of each feature based on the historical incidents:








Feature
Default weight
Reasoning




F1: Chain length
25
Present in all three incidents but varies in magnitude — weighted moderately


F2: File path repetition
30
The single most distinctive structural signal — highest weight


F3: Poster reachable
20
Critical for attack completion but may be hard to detect early in the chain


F4: Payload staged
15
Strong signal when present, but HiddenOrca had no create_file event


F5: Prior cover-up
10
Valuable but depends on having a prior incident to learn from



Total score range: 0 to 100. Default flag threshold: 60.


8.3 Computing Risk Scores for Known Incidents
The code below derives each of the five feature values from the event log for each of the three known incidents. Features F1 and F2 are continuous and normalised to [0, 1] before weighting. Features F3, F4, and F5 are binary (0 or 1), meaning they contribute either their full weight or nothing.
The final score for any incident is:

Score = (w1 × F1) + (w2 × F2) + (w3 × F3) + (w4 × F4) + (w5 × F5)

where w1…w5 are the user-specified weights summing to 100, and F1…F5 are the normalised feature values.


Show code
# ── Feature 1: Chain length score ───────────────────────────────────────────
# Each incident's hop count is divided by the maximum observed hop count
# (186 for SwiftWren) to produce a value in [0, 1].
# SwiftWren scores 1.0, HiddenOrca ~0.21, MellowOtter ~0.05.
chain_lengths <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(n_hops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(f1_chain_length = n_hops / max(n_hops))

# ── Feature 2: File path repetition rate ────────────────────────────────────
# In all three incidents the same file path appears in every relay hop,
# so repetition rate equals chain length. Normalised the same way as F1.
# For a future unknown incident this would be computed as:
#   (count of identical args.path events) / max_observed_repetitions
path_repetition <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(n_hops = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(f2_repetition = n_hops / max(n_hops))

# ── Feature 3: Recipient has posting history ─────────────────────────────────
# Build the set of all agents who have ever executed a saidit_post or flex_post.
# Then check whether any recipient (to_person) in each incident's chain
# is a member of that set. Binary: 1 if yes, 0 if no.
posters_history <- events %>%
  filter(short_name %in% c("saidit_post", "flex_post")) %>%
  mutate(poster = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:"))) %>%
  distinct(poster) %>%
  pull(poster)

posting_agents <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    f3_poster_reachable = any(to_person %in% posters_history),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(f3_poster_reachable = as.numeric(f3_poster_reachable))

# ── Feature 4: Payload file created within 30 min before chain start ─────────
# For MellowOtter and SwiftWren, payload_creations records the creation time.
# If that creation occurred 0-30 minutes before the first relay hop, F4 = 1.
# HiddenOrca has no create_file event (externally injected), so F4 = 0.
chain_starts <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(chain_start = min(datetime), .groups = "drop")

f4_payload_staged <- payload_creations %>%
  mutate(incident_name = str_remove(created_file, "\\.txt$")) %>%
  left_join(chain_starts, by = c("incident_name" = "incident")) %>%
  mutate(
    mins_before = as.numeric(difftime(chain_start, datetime, units = "mins")),
    f4_staged   = as.numeric(mins_before >= 0 & mins_before <= 30)
  ) %>%
  select(incident = incident_name, f4_staged)

f4_all <- tibble(incident = c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")) %>%
  left_join(f4_payload_staged, by = "incident") %>%
  mutate(f4_staged = replace_na(f4_staged, 0))

# ── Feature 5: Prior cover-up behaviour ──────────────────────────────────────
# Identify any agent who has previously deleted a file within 10 seconds of
# making a post (i.e. a prior cover-up event in the log).
# The inner_join matches each post event to delete events by the same agent,
# then filters to those within 10 seconds. Binary: 1 if any chain recipient
# has this history, 0 otherwise.
coverup_agents <- events %>%
  filter(short_name == "saidit_post") %>%
  mutate(
    poster    = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:")),
    post_time = datetime
  ) %>%
  select(poster, post_time) %>%
  inner_join(
    events %>%
      filter(short_name == "delete_file") %>%
      mutate(deleter = map_chr(parties, ~ str_remove(.x[[1]], "^Agent/person:"))) %>%
      select(deleter, del_time = datetime),
    by = c("poster" = "deleter")
  ) %>%
  filter(abs(as.numeric(difftime(del_time, post_time, units = "secs"))) <= 10) %>%
  distinct(poster) %>%
  pull(poster)

f5_coverup <- chains %>%
  group_by(incident) %>%
  summarise(
    f5_coverup = as.numeric(any(to_person %in% coverup_agents)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# ── Combine all features into one risk feature matrix ────────────────────────
risk_scores_base <- chain_lengths %>%
  left_join(path_repetition, by = c("incident", "n_hops")) %>%
  left_join(posting_agents,  by = "incident") %>%
  left_join(f4_all,          by = "incident") %>%
  left_join(f5_coverup,      by = "incident")

# Display the raw feature matrix before weighting
risk_scores_base %>%
  select(
    Incident              = incident,
    `F1: Chain length`    = f1_chain_length,
    `F2: Repetition rate` = f2_repetition,
    `F3: Poster reachable`= f3_poster_reachable,
    `F4: Payload staged`  = f4_staged,
    `F5: Cover-up history`= f5_coverup
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Raw feature values per incident before weighting (continuous features in [0,1], binary features 0 or 1)")



Raw feature values per incident before weighting (continuous features in [0,1], binary features 0 or 1)










Incident
F1: Chain length
F2: Repetition rate
F3: Poster reachable
F4: Payload staged
F5: Cover-up history




HiddenOrca
0.210
0.210
1
0
1


MellowOtter
0.054
0.054
1

1


SwiftWren
1.000

1

1






Code Details
F1 and F2 are both normalised using the maximum observed value across incidents, making them relative rather than absolute measures. This means if a future incident has a longer chain than any seen before, the historical scores would be re-normalised downward — the model is designed to be recalibrated as new incidents are observed. F3, F4, and F5 are binary flags: the weight is either fully applied or not applied at all.



8.4 Visualisation 9 — Risk Score Calculator
Enter custom weights for each of the five features in the input boxes below. Weights do not need to sum to 100 — the chart will display scores using the entered values directly so the effect of each weight can be explored independently. The red dashed line marks the flag threshold. The default values reflect the recommended starting configuration derived from the Q1 and Q2 analysis.


Show code
# Precompute scores for a grid of weight combinations for plotly
# Default weights
w_default <- c(25, 30, 20, 15, 10)

score_data <- risk_scores_base %>%
  mutate(
    score_default = w_default[1] * f1_chain_length +
                    w_default[2] * f2_repetition +
                    w_default[3] * f3_poster_reachable +
                    w_default[4] * f4_staged +
                    w_default[5] * f5_coverup
  )

# Build an interactive bar chart with plotly
# Since plotly sliders in R are complex, we show a sensitivity table
# and a bar chart of default scores, then a weight-sensitivity line chart

# Bar chart: default risk scores
p_risk_bar <- plot_ly(
  score_data,
  x    = ~incident,
  y    = ~score_default,
  type = "bar",
  color = ~incident,
  colors = incident_colours,
  hovertemplate = "<b>%{x}</b><br>Risk score: %{y:.1f}<extra></extra>"
) %>%
  layout(
    title  = list(text = "Risk Scores Under Default Weights",
                  font = list(size = 16)),
    xaxis  = list(title = "Incident"),
    yaxis  = list(title = "Risk score (0-100)", range = c(0, 105)),
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line", x0 = -0.5, x1 = 2.5,
      y0 = 60, y1 = 60,
      line = list(color = "#e41a1c", dash = "dash", width = 2)
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = 2.4, y = 62, text = "Flag threshold (60)",
      showarrow = FALSE, font = list(color = "#e41a1c", size = 11)
    )),
    showlegend = FALSE
  )

p_risk_bar







Observations
Under default weights, all three incidents score above the 60-point flag threshold, validating the model against the known historical cases. The file repetition rate (weight 30) and chain length (weight 25) together account for 55 points of the maximum score. Reducing either below 10 causes MellowOtter — the shortest chain — to fall below the threshold, suggesting these two features are essential for catching shorter, faster attacks.



8.5 Visualisation 10 — Weight Sensitivity Analysis
This chart shows how each incident’s risk score changes as a single feature weight is varied from 0 to 50, with the remaining weight budget redistributed equally across the other four features. It reveals which features exert the most influence over whether a chain crosses the flag threshold.


Show code
feature_names <- c("F1: Chain length", "F2: File repetition",
                   "F3: Poster reachable", "F4: Payload staged",
                   "F5: Prior cover-up")

weight_seq <- seq(0, 50, by = 5)

sensitivity_rows <- list()
for (fi in 1:5) {
  for (w in weight_seq) {
    remaining <- (100 - w) / 4
    weights   <- rep(remaining, 5)
    weights[fi] <- w

    row_scores <- risk_scores_base %>%
      mutate(
        score = weights[1] * f1_chain_length +
                weights[2] * f2_repetition +
                weights[3] * f3_poster_reachable +
                weights[4] * f4_staged +
                weights[5] * f5_coverup,
        feature        = feature_names[fi],
        feature_weight = w
      ) %>%
      select(incident, feature, feature_weight, score)

    sensitivity_rows <- append(sensitivity_rows, list(row_scores))
  }
}

sensitivity_df <- bind_rows(sensitivity_rows)

p_sensitivity <- plot_ly()

incidents_list <- c("HiddenOrca", "MellowOtter", "SwiftWren")

for (inc in incidents_list) {
  for (feat in feature_names) {
    df_sub <- sensitivity_df %>%
      filter(incident == inc, feature == feat)

    p_sensitivity <- p_sensitivity %>%
      add_trace(
        data        = df_sub,
        x           = ~feature_weight,
        y           = ~score,
        type        = "scatter",
        mode        = "lines+markers",
        name        = inc,
        legendgroup = inc,
        showlegend  = (feat == feature_names[1]),
        line        = list(color = incident_colours[inc]),
        marker      = list(color = incident_colours[inc], size = 5),
        text        = ~paste0(inc, "<br>Feature: ", feat,
                               "<br>Weight: ", feature_weight,
                               "<br>Score: ", round(score, 1)),
        hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
        visible     = if (feat == feature_names[1]) TRUE else "legendonly"
      )
  }
}

p_sensitivity <- p_sensitivity %>%
  layout(
    title      = list(text = "Score Sensitivity: How Each Feature Weight Affects the Final Score",
                      font = list(size = 15)),
    xaxis      = list(title = "Feature weight (0-50, others redistributed equally)"),
    yaxis      = list(title = "Risk score (0-100)", range = c(0, 105)),

Observations
The sensitivity chart shows that F1 (chain length) and F2 (file repetition) have the steepest score gradients — small changes to their weights produce large changes in the final score, particularly for SwiftWren (the longest chain). F3 (poster reachable) has a flat gradient for HiddenOrca and MellowOtter because those chains also reached posting-capable agents, so increasing F3’s weight lifts all three incidents equally. F5 (prior cover-up) has the smallest impact because it is binary and all three incidents share the same value for it.


Implications
Organisations with a high volume of legitimate long relay chains, such as automated pipeline orchestration systems, may need to reduce the chain length weight to avoid false positives, compensating by increasing the file repetition rate weight. Organisations that have already restricted posting permissions can reduce the poster-reachable weight, as that control is already enforced at the system level. The flag threshold can also be adjusted: a lower threshold increases sensitivity (catching more attacks) at the cost of more false positives, while a higher threshold reduces noise but risks missing shorter or faster attacks like MellowOtter.
